div.head: MARY OF MAGDALA.
div.p: MARY OF MAGDALA.

The subject of my poem was a native of Magdala, a little village on the west of the sea of Galilee, north of Tiberias. It was this Mary who bathed the Saviour's feet with her tears, and wiped them with her hair; and to her was accorded the inestimable privilege of being the first person to whom He showed Himself alive after his resurrection. Her birthplace is now a miserable ruin known to the Arabs as Mijdel but her memory is still enshrined in the hearts of all who love the Lord.
'Twas early yet, and starless gloom On Salem's city lay: When Mary sought the lonely tomb Where her dead Master lay.
And as she passed, with quickened iread, The spot where he was slain ; The empty Cross so grim, so dread, Revived her tears again.

The garden-grave was reached anon, The napkins all were there ; But 0, the Lord himself had gone. And Mary knew not where. But peering through the sombre shade, With sorrow •sore opprest ; She saw where loving hands had laid Hie body down to rest.
And, all unwilling to depart., She lingered on Ape scene; As if 'twere soothing to her heart, To be where he had been.
At last upon her startled ear The name of Mary fell ;- 0 Joy the Lord himself Was near, Whose voice she knew so well.

But 0, she might not touch him now, No more embrace his feet ; Nor to his wounded side and brow, Apply her ointment sweet. Yet still, by strong devotion moved, All gladly, at his word, She ran to tell the flock he loved, That she had seen the Lord Yes, he who died from death to save Had triumphed in the strife; And made the dark and lonesome grave. The way to endless life.
Easter, 1903.
J. H. W. CLINDINNING

div.p: The Examiner, Thursday, April 9, 1903.
THE NIGHT OF THE CRIME.
with it in the least. There was one scoundrel. and he was a friend. I agree with Tait's theory." "I don't," retorted the doctor. "Tait is au

ass." Gillard glared at the man who dared to differ from him. Tait is a clever and zealous officer. "and I believe he will capture the murderer." "He thinks he has done so, Colonel. He is fully convinced that Will is guilty. I admit that! the evidence is against the poor fellow, but I do not believe for a moment that he would do such a thing. If he had shot Tremewsn I might credit the crime. But to strangle a man in cold blood—"

"Pith 1" retorted Gillazd ; "you don't know of what knavery human nature is capable. I don't say Hannaford is guilty. All the same, things look black against him." "They do indeed, father," sighed Sue, who entered at this moment ; "buil I am sare that Dora will save him yet." "If anyone can, she is the woman," said the Colonel, who admired Dora; "a beautiful, high- spirited creature by gad, living with, a devil and a fool."

'Who is the fool, father ? " asked Sue, smiling. "Need you ask? That. baby-facer, golden- haired, silly—" "Oh! You mean Mrs. Tremewan," put ig the doctor, aIIXiOUS to cut short the many adjec- tives of the Colonel," and the devil ?" "Mrs. Bedowen," replied Gillard, without any adjectives at all; "she. is a, venomous reptile, that woman. You see sin written all over her face." " Oolcm4 ! Colonel !" protested Pascoe, with a glance at Sue. "Humph ! I -forzot that babes and suckling were present. But I can't stand Mrs. Bedceven. I believe she killed the man herself." Both Sue and Pascoe laughed. The idea was too ridiculous even for the Colonel. "If she did she has been a fool," said the doctor, " for she has lost a good place by his

death.;' "Not she !" said Gillard with supreme dis- dain. "Why Mrs. Tremewan cannot do without her. She will still rule the roost." At this !moment Mrs. Gillard entered with some hot cakes, which the Colonel loved, and which she alone could make. She heard the last speech, and uttered a feeble protest. "Indeed. Frederick, you are wrong," said she, " Mrs- Beclowen has already left the Gray House." "I don't believe it," grumbled the Colonel;' then seeing from the faces of Pascoe and Sue that the news was true, he changed the subject, by attacking his wife. "These cakes are burnt: he roared; ." Good heavens, madam, will you never learn to cook !" "Will you have your tea strong, Frederick?" said his wife, passing over the question of the cakes; for she knew that protest was vain. "I'll have any tea as I always have it, Sophia. If you make it wrong—" he eyed her grimly. and Mrs. Gillard quaked. "Well, doctor, what about Mrs. Bedowen leaving the Treraewan's ?" "I don't know much about it, Colonel." "I do," said Sue. sitting down after handing Pascoe his tea. "Mrs. Tremewan turned her out. She always hated her. At least she said so.t,

"And told a lie, I have no doubt," blustered Ginerd. 'Good heavens! the women has been her right hand all these years." "Mr. Tremewan's right hand, Frederick." "Don't contradict me, madam. Don't I know what I am talking about? I say that Mrs. Tre- mewan was under the thumb of that house- keeper." "Well, she isn't under it now," said Sna, pertly; "she has gone to live at Salcombe on her annuity." " Annuity ! Who gave the damned woman an annuity' ?" "She received it under the .Iyill of her late master," said Sue, complacently. "Dora has told me all about it. The will was read a few days ago. Mrs. Tremewan gets all the money and the house for her life, and after her death it goes to Dora. But she has•to pay to Mrs. Bedowen an annuity of £2OO a year." "How nice for Mrs. Bedowen," said kindly Mrs. Gillard. The Colonel fell on her. "You dare to say that, madam, and you know what a demon that housekeeper is! lam sure she extorted the annuity. If I had my way I'd put her in gaol— on bread and water, with hard Labour. I dare. say she has been in gaol; she looks like it." , "My dear Colonel !" laughed Pascoe. "You will be had tep for libel." "By that woman, sir T- Never ! She is a female With a past. If she went into court her character would be gone. Ha! So she has an annuity has she? I always said Tremewan was a fool. Why has she one to Saloombe ?" "She intends to take in boarders." "Begad she will," said the Colonel, grimly "and in more senses than one. I am sorry for the boarders. She'll murder them in their beds." "Frederick ! Frederick !" "I say she will. Taken a cottage has she ? Humph ! I hope the landlord will get his rent." "She has taken a very pretty cottage," said Sue. "You remember, mother, that one by Bolt Head. I daresey she'll do very well. Dora said there was a great row, and that Mrs. Tremewau gave Mrs. Bedowen her opinion." And I expect Mrs. Bedowen returned the compliment," said the doctor. "Indeed no. She said nothing. She listened to all her mistress had to say, then made only. one observation in fore leaving the room." "Ha, ! So like a woman," growled the Colonel, "will have the last word, begad. I'll bet it was something insolent." "No !" replied Sue, doubtfully, "I don't think it was very insolent." "What did she say ? out with it, Sue." "She said. 'Mr, Tremewan, whew, death I sincerely deplore, has left pie sufficient to live upon. I will theref are accept my dismissal. Of your opinion of me I have no remark to make. Good-day." "What a wonderful memory you have, Sue," said her mother admiringly ; "those are her very words, I expect. And well chosen too." Gillard glared at his wife, and opened his mouth to make a crushing speech. However, she met his furious gaze so meekly, that he changed his mind and spoke generally. "I call it a most insolent speech," he cried, "she's an infernal witch. Dishonesty and deceit and impudence are written all over her face. If I had been Mrs. Tremewan I should have searched her boxes. She is sure to have stolen something. That class of woman always does. What is she going to do now ?" "I told you father. Take a cottage and—" "Oh, yes. Boarders ! What a come down. But she's a good cook I hear—a very good cook. I wish she'd set up a class in Dartbridge, then you two could take lessons. I'm poisoned in this house." The Colonel paused, then, as he could think of nothing else disagreeable, he changed the subject. "What abeut Vane ?" "Vane—Frederick. Who is Vane ?" "You're a fool, Sophia—you always are. Vane

is—', Here Pascoe, sorry for Mrs. Gillard, interposed. "Paul Vane is the son of Tremewan's sister, I believe," he said; "he lives in London, and is an artist—" "I knew he was something damned idiotic," grumbled Gillard. Mrs. Gillard reflected; "I remember now," she said, in her meek way; "he was here many years ago. Not at all a tbad looking young man, hut with very little of the Tremewan fire in him. If I. recollect rightly, he did not altogether agree with his uncle.' ." Who could agree with Mr. Tremewan ?" asked Sue, oonternptuously. "I could," said her father sharply. "I never had a word with Tremewan. When he tried to bully me, I gave my opinion of his insolence. He did not dare to contradict me, so we got on very well. As for Paul Vane, ,he was, and I da,resay is—a blithering, idiot. He and his uncle had a great row. but Vane couldn't hold his own. Tre- mewan sent him off with a flea in his ear, and they never spoke again. Ha 1" said Gillard, rubbing his nose, "I shouldn't wonder if he killed Tremewan." "Colonel Colonel 1" protested the doctor, laughing. "you accuse everyone. Some people must be innocent" "I don't accuse you, doctor. But if Tremewan. had been your patient, I _might have done so.. Ha! Ha! Don't be angry, Pascoe—only my joke. But this Vane. He was stopping at the Nelson Hotel the other day. I shouldn't be surprised if he had something to do with the matter."

"Impossible !" said Mrs. Gillard, with a firm- ness .foreign to her; "from what I recollect of Mr. Vane he would not have killed a fly." "Flies dun't leave money, .Sophia." "But that Aloft, not matter," cried Sue; "in any case, Mr. Vane, whatever his relationship, could not have inherited." "No ! No ! lin,: said be could have." snorted

bar tatle,r; "c-ftib..- nonsense, Sue. But lln not surprised. Mrs. Tremewan and her daughter have the estates, and quite right too. And that cat of a housekeeper is at Salcombe. Ha! All very nicely settled. But what about Will Hanna- ford, poor wretch ?" "He is in prison, Frederick," said Mrs. Oil- lard, timidly. "Of course he is in prison. Do you take me for a fool, Sophia. What I mean is, how long will he stay there ? "
_ "Until Dora and Mr. Hannaford can get him out."
"Pooh I pooh I tell you the young fellow is guilty. He will never get out till they hang him at
"Colonel, don't!" Mrs. Gillard grew white. "You accused. Vane just now, Colonel," said Pascoe; "in your opinion, who is guilty, may I ask ?"

"God bless me, Pascoe, how should I know. Tait says that the evidence is stiong against this young fellow, and Tait ought to know his busi- ness. If not he should be removed as an in- competent ass. I am sorry for Will. A good lad as lads go. But he shouldn't strangle people. One always gets into trouble if they do that sort of thing. He is sure to be hanged." "Father ! father !" cried Sue, her eyes filling with tears; "don't. Poor Will, so young and handsome. And Dora, think of Dora." "I'm very Sorry for her, and for him," said the Colonel, testily, and rather ashamed of him- self; "I don't wish them any ill. But Tait—l believe in Tait—" "I don't," put in Pascoe, "he's a conceited ass."

"I think so, too," sobbed Sue; "and Will shan't be hanged. Dora is sure to save him." "I hope so, I'm sure. There, there, Sue, don't cry. If Will is condemned I'll get up a petition, asking for commutation of sentence." Bat, the Colone' shook his head, "he is sure to be hanged." "I don't agree with you," said Pascoe, and the Colonel glared. "Dear me !" said Mrs. Gillard, to make peace, "I wonder which if you will be right in the end." "What an idiot you are, Sophia !" snorted thi gallant Co/onel.

div.head: CHIPTER XL
div.p: CHIPTER XL
GOSSIP.

Ch lone' Gilland arid his family dwelt in a roomy house on the side of a windy hill. The mansion waa napeosed to be haunted, and for that reason the Colonel rented it cheap. Whether these were any ghosts or not it is hard to say. Mrs. Gillard declared that she heard ltifiSeB and saw "things" in the twilight, but she did not count—at least with her husband—so what she said went for nothing. The Colonel himself had no nerves, and no superstition; his six children took after him ; therefore as regards the supernatural they were fairly happy; always, of course, with the exception of Mrs. Gillard aforesaid. The Colonel was a desperately poor ex-army officer long since retired. Dartbridge being the least costly place he could find in the three king- doms, he lived there and grumbled constantly at being compelled to do so. His five7boys were all booked for the army, but as yet were too young to leave the nest. Sue, it was supposed, would be married, although there were as yet no signs of matrimony about her. But her father was break- ing her in to be the slave of a ..friture husband, and her mother was teaching her to look after the house. The Gillards kept no servant, and only on extreme occasions was Mrs. Bennett the charwoman called in. And then the Colonel raged so much about the expense that Mrs. Gilled and Sue were glad to get her out of the house again. The poor wife was; faded woman, who had been a beauty. Colonel Gillard had married her for her looks, and when these were gone he grumbled because slip had lost them. He fre- quently reminded her that she had brought him no money, and was not worth her keep; and Mrs. Gillard never contradicted him. All the spirit she possessed, and that was not much, had long since been bullied out of her. The Colonel, was a stout, red-faced man, who gobbled like a turkey cock, was almost always in, a passion. He had lived in India the greater part of his life, and was devoted to curries of the hottest. For this reason he never behaved amiably. Yet he thought himself the best of men, and esteemed the rest of his fellow mortals fools and knaves. He regarded his wife as something still lower, and never hesitated to tell her his candid opinion: of he.r intellect. Sue did what she could to de- fend her mother, but usually got the worst of it. Shortly after the inquest and the arrest of Will, Dr. Pascoe called in one evening to play• • whist. A game with the Colonel was not the choicest sort of amusement a. man could have, but Jack Pascoe was attracted to the house by Sue. He was falling in love with this red-haired freckled faced girl, and frequently caught him- self thinking how she would look at a breakfast table vis-a-vis with himself. Mrs. Gillard saw that the young doctor was attracted, and as he was a clever man and of good family she was pleased for her daughter's sake. She often pitied Sue for the wretched life she led, and much as she would miss her, did her best to for- ward the wooing. Sue herself had some ides of the doctor's admiration, but thought that the happiness of becoming his wife was too good to be true. The five boys and their father saw nothing • if they had, Dr. Pascoe would have been k 44 out of the house. They did not wish to lose one of their white slaves. It is but just to my that owing to the example of the Colonel the boys regarded the status of their mother and sister as the natural position of woman. They were fond of them both, but they -"did not re- spect them. How could they when their father so frequently expressed his contempt for the sex? After a good dinner cooked by Mrs. Gillard and Sue, the Colonel and his guest settled down with wife and daughter to whist. The five boys crept out of the room. They knew what whist meant, and gave their father a wide berth. Sometimes they were made to play, and then the Colonel only stopped short of actual murder. On this occasion, in compliment. to the doctor, he was given Sue for a partner, and Gillard played with his unhappy wife. She W 2.3 so nervous under his eye that she made mistakes all through the game, and submitted to be sworn at in silence. Not even the presence of Pascoe could mitigate the rancour of the Colonel's tongue. His conver- sation—or rather the monologue he indulged in— was dramatic in the extreme.
"Do I lead'?" timid voice.
asked Mrs. Gillard, in her weak

"Of course you do, madam," thtmdered the: Colonel, "don't you know the game ?. Where are your brains! Now, why did you lead that? Hearts are trumps—you know they are—yet, confound you, madam, you lead spades, etc.' "I think Mrs. Gillaird is right, Colonel," ven- tured the doctor.
" Ah, I suppose you do," grumbled the other; "dunned chivalry. If you had her for a part- ner you wouldn't say so. . • There you are— an ace."
"Our trick, Frederkk," said Mrs. Gillard with a weak laugh. "How can you be surs of that, I .only took it with an ace," sneereA Gillard. "Is it nay lead ?" asked !Sue picking up her cards.

"If you don't pa.y attention you'd better leave the table. Clubs ! Ah, I thought so. Now, madam," cried the Colonel, slapping his cards on the table, "do you see what you have done ?" "No, Colonel. What have I done! Oh, that ! Well, I'm sure I couldn't help it." Then mimed a pause, during which Mrs. Gillard made another mistake, and protested feebly, "If only knew what cards you have, Frederick !"

"-Oh, Lord," groaned the Colonel, rising in a fury. "I can't play any more. I shan't. have a fit begad. Get the supper Sophia. We'll finish the game on another rught, when your brain is clearer." Mrs. Gillard was not at all put out by all this, nor was the doctor. It is true when he first entered into the bosom of this
family he found these domestic scenes rather trying, but custom is everything, and he simply Nast silent until the storm blew over. He and the

Colonel lighted- their cigars, and sat down on either side of the fire-place while Sue and her mother went to bring in the tea and cake. Gillard haying no ono to storm at, (condescended to talk sensibly. "Well, dector," he said amiably; "and what do you think of the chances of Will ITatuutford ?" "q don't know about his chances, Colonel; but I am sure he is innocent." "If he wasn't I shouldn't blame him," roared Gillard. " Tremewan was an overbearing beast, sir. No wanners--absolutely none. I wonder he was not murdered long ago. I honour the man who strangled him, by gad T do 1" • "Then you don't honour Will Hannoford," re- plied Pascoe, decisively. "He is not ,c_cuilty. I was at the inquest, and I believe every word of his story." "Then if he isn't innocent, who is guilty ? Answer me that, sir." "I can't tell you the name of the person or persons Colonel, but—" "Hey 1" cried Gillard, getting redder than ever; 'you speak in the plural." " Well, you see, Colonel, it is my opinion that Stem is mere than one person concerned in this ' matter. It is only a theory of mine, but I fancy that those who stretched the rope across the road to kill Will also murdered Tremewan. They wished to bag both birds at once, but Will escaped." "He escaped them." said the Colonel, grimly, "only to die by the hands of the hangmen; They —uhoeyer they are—must. be pleased." "I don't think Will Hannaford will be hanged,' : said Pascoe, quietly. "Public opinion is with

him." "Just because he gave himself up?" "Partly that, and partly because be 'is en: gaged to marry Dora Tremewan. If he wishes to marry the girl, he certainly cannot be guilty of the death of her father."

"Humph ! Nothing new has been found?" No. But I understand that Miss Tremewan and Hannaford are working together. I hope they will find the rascals." "'Why do you think there is more than one ?"t , asked the Colonel, curiously. I "I only judge from the way in which he waa ! murdered. I think that one man held him in conversation while the other slipped the cord over his her Ad. It is merely a theory." "Al] wrona," .srrowlecl Gillard: don't azreed

div.head: CHAPTER XII
div.p: CHAPTER XII
DORA TREMEWAN, DETECTIVE.

A woman so shallow as Mrs. Tremewan could hot mourn long. While it lasted, her grief was violent and noisy • but when her late husband was placed in the family vault, she dried her tears. The will having been read, Mrs.. Bedowen having been got rid of and mourning having been ordered, Mrs. Tremewan began to sigh for a change. "It is so dull here, Dora," she said one even- lag; "don't you think we had better take a run up to town?" We are in mourning, mother," said Dora with some stiffness.

"Oh, my dear, as if I didn't know that. But you are such au impossible girl, quite impossible. I always said so. Of oourse, I mourn my poor sear Francis, who was the joy of my life, but it is useless for me to spoil my looks with tears. I am sure Francis would not wish me to. He was always so particular about my eyes being red." Here she paused, not because she had exhausted her subject such as it was, but because she was out of breath with her aimless babble.

Dora looked at her helplessly. She did not know how to manage this fool, for that her mother certainly was. Mrs. Tremewan had no ideas in her bead save a desire to preserve her beauty and enjoy her life. Dora could not follow her in all the wanderings of her mind, for she usually began on one subject and ended with another quite different, after the method of Prade's vicar. On the present occasion Dora understood what she was aiming at, but pretended not to understand. She did not think it right that Mrs. Tremewan should emerge from her seclusion so soon after the death of her husband. There was a fitness in all things, and Dora said as much, with some indignation. Mrs. Tremewan grew_ angry.

- "Oh, iroourse that is all very well, but you don't know how this gloomy house gets on my nerves. I require gaiety and bright companion- ship.. If you were only a different sort of girl I could put up with the place for a few months. I'm sure I don't wish to do anything people will think strange, not that it matters. But I won't stay here. I haven't get so many years of life before me that I can afford to waste any shut up in a vault like this. I want enjoyment, and thote is no reason why I should not have it. We have plenty of money." "Mother," said Dora as quietly as she could in the face of this revolting selfishness; "my father has not been dead a month ! If you went up to London people would talk. Can you not wait for six months ?" "I shall be dead if I stay here all that time,"
"Men will you go to Torquay ? " "At this season of the year? Certainly not. There is not a: soul about."

"Ah !" said Dora, bitterly; "it is society you wish for, mother." "And why not ?" complained Mrs. Tremewan. "It is bad for me to be. alone. lam Sure I loved Francis, but I can't be always thinking about him. If he was alive would be the first per- son to take me away to a, more cheerful place. But you don't understand me, Dora; you never will." "Well, mother, you are your own mistress. Go to London if you like." "I mn't go alone. It would not be proper. Be- sides you are better than nobody, and now that Mrs Bedowen has gone we can leave the house with perfect safety. She was a cat; I believe she stole tbings. I don't know why Francis had her in the house. I never liked her; yet she was here for years, as you know. It was the only thing. Francis would never let me have my own way about. I said again and again 'Send her away,' but he would not."

"She is out of the house now; say no more about her, mother." "That is so like you, Dora, when you knew it relieves me to speak. I have no one to open my mind to. If Mr Hannaford—George, you know —was only as kind as he used to be, he would call and see me."

"He has his own trouble, poor man," said Dora, with a sigh. "His troubles are nothing to mine. He has not lost a husband"; and Mrs. Tremewan put a dainty, black-edged handkerchief to her eyes. "His son is in prison." "And so he ought to be, after killing your poor dear-" Mother !" Dora rose, tall and stern, from her chair and stood over the whimpering little woman like an accusing angel. "Never say that again ! I am as certain as I Stand here that Will did not kill my father."

"The jury and M. Tait say that he did," replied Mrs. Tremewan "It is not the truth. I know what people say, but they are all fools. I love Will, and I intend to marry him." "Indeed !" said the widow, with an angry look in her blue eyes; "and how do you proposed to save him from being hanged ?".

„ Dora winced. She saw that she had an enemy in her niother. Like all weak .people, Mrs. Tre- mewan always sided with the majority. Almost everyone thought that Will was guilty, and the • widow agreed with them. She never wei2hud the pros and cons of the question herself. She took her opinions as she did her religion—ready- made. However, Dora knew the futility of argu- ing the question so she simply contented herseli with .an explanation. "I intend to help Mr. Hannaford to save his son,” said she in a calm voice; "and I am glad you spoke of the matter, mother. I shall not leave Dartbridge until Will is released from prison and stands clear of any accusation that can be brought against him." "And you won't come to London," said Mrs. Tremewan, angrily. • "No." In the first place I think you should stay in seclusion, and in the second I have to be on the spot to see about Will." "So selfish," moaned the widow, wringing her hands; "always thinking of yourself instead of your lonely mother. But I shall not emulate you, my heartless child. I shall remain here until thle.man is free or hanged." "He will not be hanged," said Dora, her cheek turning white. "But lam glad von have decided to stay, mother." "I know my duty:, I hope, Dora," said Mrs. Tremewan . with dignity. "'or you to think of going tO London at this juncture would be fairly indecent. Let us say no more about it I beg. I have my deceased darling to think of." In this masterly fashion Mrs. Tremewan turned the tables on her daughter.. Dora never thought of arguing the point. She was only to pleased that her mother had given way with so little persuasion. For the next few days the widow prided herself on her self-denial, and made Ire-
amnions to ner reermgs. roor sirs. tin- lard moo over to see her, and was detained for an_hour, while Mrs. Tremewan detailed all _ .
her guffcrinis,.and dLseussed the new mourning.
Dora was aCot. in the house on this occaion. She

iad gone over to see Mr. Hannaford.. Ever since the inquest these two had become great friends. Hannaford. -never spoke of Tre- meavan, or of Ms enmity towards him, and he rarely mentioned Mrs. Tremewan. But Dora he grew to love, and he gave her all the affection of a lonely man. Besides, he felt that the posi- tion of Will had in a measure been brought about by his own selfishness. For if he had not ordered Will to remain absent from Dart)aidg,e on pain of losing his inheritance, the poor lad would never have paid that secret visit which had resulted so lamentably. He said as much to Dora when she called to see him. And the visit was paid while Mrs. Gillas.d was listening to the 'railings of the widow.

Mr.-Hannaford, looked much older than he had done when Dora first saw him. He was a proud Man, and moreover, in spite of his severity, loved his son.. That Will should be in gaol on a mimi- ng"l charge was a source of grief to him, and he felt that he would never be able to hold up his head again. The shame was too great. "It is all my fault, my dear," he said to the girl. "I should have consented to your marrying Will, and then he would not have gone away. Oh ! I wish you had called to see me before your father died.'

"You would not have received me," said Dora, with a sigh. "Perhaps I should not, my dear. I have been very foolish. My action with regard to Will only resulted in his concealing his presence in Dartbridge on that night; and thus lending colour to the accusation of Tait and others. I am- bound to say that the whole circumstances are suspicious on the face of them. Bub you understand the reason, my dear. My fault." "I know that Will came secretly so that he should not lose his inheritance," said Dora ; "he said as much to me in a letter. But I cannot understand why he should have called on my father at all." Mr. Hannaford shook his head. "I cannot find but that," he said; "I have seen Will several times. He bears up well, poor fellow, and is willing to telling me most things. But on that point he is dumb." "Do you think he would tell me," asked Dora, oltsping her hands. No. He declared most &item* that the matter on which he saw your father could not be told to any human being." "What could he mesa?"

"What, indeed. I can conceive nothing that your father could have done that Will should make such a secret of it. Have you any idea ?" "No. My father was a strange man," said Dora, thoughtfully; "and he had his own secrets. I wonder if Mrs. Bedowen would know," she said suddenly. Mr. Elannaford, who was walking up and down the room, turned suddenly; and they looked at one another. "That is an idea," he said, and came to seat himself beside her. "Dora," he continued after a pause, "in searching for a possible assassin I thought that I would find out who was in Daatbridge on the night of the mur- der. I fancied that some stranger might have killed my old friend, your father. Therefore, on this basis I made inquiries, or rather, I caused them to be made. I have a man in my employ called Grant, who is very sharp, and Is, more- over, devoted to Will. I sent him to find out who was in the town on the night in question. He learned that a stranger, who called himself Captain Max, was at the Eight Bells, and re- mained there all night Miss Jinney, who keeps the inn, was disinclined to speak of her lodger, and to tell you the truth she boxed Grant's ears for asking. But the lad found out what he wished to knOw from one of the maids, who had' learned more than she should have done. I under- stand that the maid has since been dismissed by Miss Jinney. That is most remarkable, my dear," ended the old man looking at Dora. Miss Tremewtm shook her head. "I don't see what the fact of a man staying at an obscure inn can have to do with my father's death. It is la-ue that a stranger might have killed him, and that this Captain Max might be the man, butt we have no proofs that there was any communi- cation between them." "Wait a moment, my dear," said Hannaford, laying his hand on hers; " Grant also discovered that Mrs. Bedowen called to see this man on that night." "Impossible !" said Dora, in surprise, "she was in bed at ten o'clock, I saw her go up the etairs." "But she was out on that night." "Yes, I think she went to see a sick friend. I 'mow she told my mother as much. But she returned in proper time, and went to Led." "Oh! she called to see this man early," replied Mr. Hannaforl, "and it seems she was with him foa some time. I have tried to find out what they spoke of, but can !earn nothing. It was your mention of Mrs. Bedowen knowing yourfather's secrets that made me refer to this fact. Do you think, Dora, that your father's death may have to do with the meeting between Mrs. Bedowen and this stranger ?" "I don't see any connection," said Dora after a pause; "I know my father trusted Mrs. Bedo- wen, and told her all his secrets. She seemed to have some kind of hold over him. I never liked: her myself, and any mother bated her. As a rule my father • always humoured my mother's whims, but when she wanted Mrs. Bedowen dismissed, be refused." "Well, there seems to be some sort of secret understanding between Mrs. Bedowen and this man, else why should she.call to see him ?" "He may be an old friend of hers," objected Dora. "Tell me, Dora, is Mrs. Bedowen a, lady?" "No. She is not even an imitation of one. She told me once in a fit of oonfidence, that she was a farme.i's daughter." "Then I tell you, my dear, that this Captain Max was a gentleman, according to what Grant heard. Now, why should a woman in Mrs. Beclowen's position call to see a gentleman at a low public-house? Moreover Dora, the name 'Captain Max' seems to be an assumed one. I don't .say that I am certain that anything may come of this. But I think if you saw Mrs. Bedowen and questioned her—" , "She would tell me nothing. She hates me." "Then I will go. I want to find out what this man was doing at Dartbridge,-and if he.han any Connection with your father." "I can't see any possible connection," replisal Miss Tremewan" ; but if anyone is to see Mrs. Bedowen I think it best for me to go. It is a forlorn hope, certainly, but Will is in such straits that I am ready to grasp at any straw. I will go over to Saleombe and see Mrs. Bedowen. What about this. man Is he still in.Darte bridge." "No. He left next morning for -Salcombe." "For Salcombe, and she is there ! That it strange." "So strange, that I believe something will oome of your visit," said the old man hopefully. "My dear," he laid his hand on Dora's arm, "we shall save my boy yet ! " "I am sure of that, Mr. Hannaford. I have never wavered in my belief that his innocence will be proved. God is good. He will not let an innocent man suffer." " Ah, my dear," was the sad reply; "how many innocent men have suffered." Dora was still unoonvince-d. " They had no ass like you to defend them, or like me for the natter of that. I shall devote my life to proving the innocence of my darling." . "How you love him, Dora "I do, better than my life. Oh, Mr. Hanna., ford, how I wish I had seen you before my father died; how I wish we could have under- stood one another then as we do now. You might then have given your consent." "I certainly should have done so. I have been hasty and foolish." "Well, I don't know. Perhaps after all it has needed this mutual sorrow to draw us together," Dora took his hand and added softly, 'lt has done that, I think." Ilan.naford kissed her hand in his courtly olsf.: fashiOned way. "You are the bravest and sweetest lady in the world," he said; "and be.: tween us we will see justice done. Go, my dear Dora, see this woman at Salcombe. But be care- ful—very careful. She is both .crafty and cunning." Dora nodded. "Yon may be sure I shall be an my grard; I know her well, and how to deal with her. Besides as she has been left an annuity by incy unhappy father, she can scarcely refura 'k avenon his death. Though, to be sure, I Oa not think she is a grateful woman." "She will do exactly what she Ihinks will her best," staid Hannaford thoughtfully. "She _ is not the woman, so far as I can gather, to let either gratitude or Late outweigh her own. Me . tereste. If she can make money she will speak. If it nava her better to be silent., she will bold

div.p: tier tongue. lOU ITIUNt be 7111lted" toy tier seasii veasation as to your best, course of action." "Do you think I ought to offer her a, bribe " "No. You could not offer one large enougla.- But if in some way you could let her • know that her annuity is not safe unless the. truth wanes to light, that would make her speak., However, it no use talking like that; she will see through an idle threat. No, Dora, after all you had better appeal to hcr feelings." "Bat you said—" .

"lii,);, -My. dear," replied Ilaimaford with a sigh; "but I do not see what else you can glie is a hard woman, but she mav yield to—" he stopped and shook his head, "I. can't advise "Let" us leave it to chance then," and Dora rose to depart. "That is best. You take up this clue of Cap-. bain Max, and I shall search for another." "Another I. What other ?" "Why, I must set Grant to work again to learn who else was in Dartbridge on that fatal. night."

7` Why not ask Colonel Gillard. He knows ever- one who comes and goes." Hannaford shook his head. "That would not be wise. The Colonel is a. great talker, and any- thing of this sort must be done quietly." .He paused, then continued, "someone called at the Gray House after my son left. I must find that person. If I succeed—" "Well, Mr. Hannaford; if you succeed !" "Will's innocence may then be proved." "It must be proved, said Dora firmly ; trust in God."
To be Continued.

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
FRIENDLY MATCH.

WARRINGTON " A" V. WIGAN "A."—Warrington "'A" were victorious on Sgturday when they encountered Wigan" A" on the Wilderspool enclosure before a large gathering of spectators. Wigan kicked off, and there being no return the first scrimmage took place in the Warrington half. A free kick to the Warringtoniana availed them little, the visitors rushing the ball to the vicinity of the home goal. A huge kick by Knight put the home team on the aggressive, and smart following up by the forwards further improved their position. By the aid of a free kick the visitors entered the home half, but the stay here was only brief:Mahoney obtained pcssession and scored a fine try,Knight adding the extra points. Exchange kicking was the order for a time until Hockenhall made a dashing run along touch, and Wigan were again forced' to adopt a defensive attitude. The visitors. by short stages managed to get a footing near the War- rington line, but nothing tangible accrued. Bailey was next seen to advantage,and was going very strong until checked at the opportune moment. Half-time: War- rington, five points; Wigan, nil. On resuming, Brooks made a splendid run, only to be grassed when nearing the line. After a spell of midfield play, the visitors' seemed like becoming dangerous until Knight stepped in and prevented disaster. Following this Warrington again threatened' danger, and Hunter receiving from a scrimmage' dropped a goal. After this reverse the visitors quickly returned to the attack, and Warrington being penalized, Bothwell kicked a goal. Each end was next visited in turn, and good work by the visitors ended in a try neat the posts. Bothwell failed at the easy place. War' rington attacked near the close, and a combined move- ment in which 'Mahoney and Hockenhall figured pro- minently, ended in the latter being pushed into touch near the corner flag. There was no further scoring, and a hard game ended in a victory for Warrington by seven points to five.

The Duchess of Wesuninster continues to make excel- lent progress towards convalescence, and all doubts as to her Grace's ability to return to Eaton Hall in order to entertain the Prince and Princes of Wales for Chester races are oow happily removed.

div.head: MISS GRACE SMITH.
div.p: MISS GRACE SMITH.

'One of the most rising pianists of the day is 'Miss Grace Smith. who for her age has attained great success. She was educated originally at • St. Margaret's School, Bushey. She was nine Years of age when it was first discovered that shepossessed any special talent tor •music: from that time on- wards she was trained with a view to her par- ticular bent. her first public success at the piano was scored at a school con- cert at the age •of thirteen, when she made a great hit by Playing a Rondo by Dussek-. She was at the time one of Madame Colmache's pu- pils; she con- 'tinned to study under her until she was twenty- one. Miss Grace Smith gave her Ir_ GRACE SMITH. 'first concert at THE WONDERFUL LADY PIANIST. the Salle-Erard, which was followed by one at Windsor, under the patronage of Princess Chris- tian, who had heard her at a school concert. Her late Majesty showed her interest in the young performer by taking tickets. Other notable people before whom Miss Smith played included: Sir Frederick Bridge, Sir Walter Parratt, Sir Hubert Parry, Dannreuther and Beringer. At .the age of twenty-one Signor Busoni heard Miss Smith, and invited her to join his class in Weimar. There she spent several months, after which she went on to Berlin and spent a year under Madame _ • Carrenm
SHAMROCK HI.

- Sir Thomas Lipton's new challenger, Sham- rock 111, which was launched by the Countess of Shaftesbury on St. Patrick's day, has already made her mark. She has sailed several tests on the Clyde with Shamrock I, which was quite as good a boat as Shamrock 11, and has proved herself a far faster boat. This week she comes down South to Wey- mouth, where further tests between the two will take place. If Shamrock 111 maintains her form, it looks as though at last the American Cup may be "lifted" and brought back to its original home after half a century of trying; and it is cordially hoped on all sides that Sir Thomas Lipton will this time meet with well-deserved success. Experts are very hopeful and far more enthusiastic than they were over the two preceeding Shamrocks. Shamrock 111 is the result of the combined wavk of Mr. Fife and Mr. Watson, designers reectively of Shamrock I and Shamrock 11, mid they have brought the lessons taught by the failure of the other two to bear upon the latest of the famous series. The new yacht is normal in the water, but finer in the bow, With increased sail and beam and greater
SHAMROCK 111, WHICH SIR THOMAS LIPTON IS CONFIDENT WILL BRING •HOME THE CUP.

length. The new defender, which is probably to be christened the Reliance, also shows in- Freased sail and beam with greater length, but In contrast is lower in the water and blunter In the bow. The latter is due to be launched within the next fortnight. Shamreck 111 and Shamrock I. have had two further trials this week. In the first, in company with the steam yacht Erin, the two cutters left Gourock shortly after ten o'clock, and reached " easy " to Rothesay Bay with jackyard topsail over main- sail, jib, and foresail. The course was a lee- ward, and windward one, twice to Largs Bay and back, finishing with a broad reach back up-channel to Cloch Lighthouse. When the spinnaker run was started, Shamrock I. had a lead of over a minute. The challenger over- hauled slowly, and midway on the six miles was abeam to leeward, in which position they ran the remainder of the stretch, the challenger coming out to the weather berth on rounding the Erin. - The beat back was all in favour of Shamrock 111., which took the windward place within a short distance, and ate away until she led by nearly three miuutes at the weather mark in Rothesay Bay. On the second run the breeze was varying a good deal, and the match suffered. At the close of this distance, Sham- rock I. had gained slightly, but she lost con- siderably again- by the wind, the difference as they bore away for the reach up - channel being nearly four minutes against her. Both had jib-topsails along the wind for about three miles, the challenger having added another minute to her lead when topsails were downed. Sir Thomas Lipton was again perfectly content with the performance, and says he has a winning boat. Shamrock 1. has been towed to South- ampton. The challenger remains until to- morrow morning, a few details having to be overhauled by the builders' workmen. The three trials have proved the new boat to be very fast by the wind in light breezes. " She has beaten Shamrock I also in reaching in a good wind. She is little better, howewer, in spinnaker work.

div.head: NEW LAND BILL.
div.p: THE NEW LAND BILL.

When he introduced the Irish Land Bill, Mr. George Wyndham was encouraged by the sym- pathy of all parties of Irishmen. A free grant of £12,000,000 is to be given in order to bridge the gap between what the tenants are expected to pay and what the landlords will accept, but the Chief Secretary holds out the hope that equivalent economies 'nay be made in other Irish departments. Judgment as to the details was reserved by Mr. John Redmond, but Colonel Saunderson spoke in a friendly tone, and only one Conservative member gave any hint of opposition on the part of British tax-
RT. HON F. WRENCH.
MR. W.
F. BAILY.
Two of the Three Commissioners under the New Bill.

payers. Already there are signs of criticism, especially over the i 2,000,000. Nationalists meantime continue the parliamentary truce. It is evident that they will do their best to provide facilities for Proceeding with the Land Bill, which they mayamend in committee. The situa- tion, so far as Ireland is concerned, impresses all parliamentary experts. Nationalist goodwill has certainly simplified the work of the Govern- ment, and particularly of the Leader of the House, to an extraordinary extent, and it has relieved the Chief Secretary from the most dis- agreeable of his duties. Mr. Wyndham by his tact has done a great deal to secure this friendliness.

div.head: OUR DISTINGUISHED CANADIAN VISITOR.
div.p: OUR DISTINGUISHED CANADIAN VISITOR.

The Hon. Clifford Sifton, who is at present on a visit to England, is Minister of the Interior and Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs for the Dominion of Canada, and is the youngest Cabinet Minister in Sir Wilfrid

Laurier's Ad- ministration. He was born in March, 1861, and although only past his fortieth year,has occupied a seat in the Dominion Cabinet since 1896. Mr. Sif- ton was called ,to the Bar in 1882, and was elected to the local Parliament of Manitoba in 1888. In 1891 he was sworn in as Attorney- General for that Province, a posi- tion which he retained until he was invited by Sir Wilfrid Lau- rier to accept his present position. His appointment as British Agent in connec- tion with the Alaska Boundary Commission is, from the point of knowledge of the con- troversy, undoubtedly the • best one that could have been made. The question of boundaries and matters of internal concern have beer, under Mr. Sifton's jurisdiction, and he has shown himself thoroughly conversant with the question in dispute. His visit to England is now in connect on with this very important matter affecting not only Canadian but British interests.

div.head: AFRICA
div.p: AFRICA
Kemball was born

in 1859, and is now only forty-three years of age. He was the son of Major-General J. S. Kemball, and was educated at Harrow. In 1878 he was gazetted to the Royal Artillery, and was promoted captain in 1886, major in 1896, and lieutenant-colonel in 1901, and now he holds the rank of brigadier-general in West Africa. He served for some years on the Head- quarters Staff in India, and has seen plenty of fighting in the course of his career. In 1879 and 1880 he went through the Afghan war, and in 1895 he was with the Chitral Relief Force, being mentioned in despatches. He was again mentioned in 1897 and 1898 during operations ons the North-West Frontier of India. Then he joined the West African Frontier Force in 1901, and commanded the expedition against Kontagora and Bida, for which he was rewarded with the D. 5.0., a medal and a clasp. Both• Sir Frederick Lugard and he are expected home next month. With the occupation of Sokoto, Katsena, and Kano, the military operations, which commenced on Jan. 29, when Colonel Morland left the ad- vanced post of Zaria for Kano, may be hre- garded as at an end. There is now no impor- tant hostile centre in Hausaland. In a con- siderable shorter period than was anticipated, and with much less fighting than even the most sanguine expected, the greatest remain- ing hostile centres in Northern Nigeria have been brought under control. Thus, within a period of about twelve months almost the whole of the vast area included in the northern portion of: the Protectorate, with a frontier of something like f poo miles, has been traversed by British forces, and brought under effective control. The troops under General Kemball and Colonel Morland in less than one month marched over 250 miles through hostile, unknown, and largely waterless country. It is a significant fact that although the great hostile Fulani, centres were occupied, the Emirs of Sokoto and Kano, ,together with the murderer of Capt. Moloney, all bolted. The news-of the fall of Sokoto came over the French telegraph line from Say

div.head: STRANGE BEQUEST. The Story of the Bridgwater Trust
div.p: A STRANGE BEQUEST. The Story of the Bridgwater Trust

The following sketch appears in the current number of the "Golden Penny :—" The story of the Bridg- water Trust" affords one more proof of the fact that truth is stranger than fiction. In 1736 Francis Egerton, the third and last Baron Bridgwater, was born. As a young man he was much interested in the subject of inland navigation, and in 1758 he set about con- structing the first canal in England—that con- necting Worsley with Manchester and Runcorn. The scheme required a large working capital, and in order to provide the necessary funds the Earl reduced his personal expenses to the lowest possible sum. His enterprise in this and other direc- tions was rewarded with great success, and he amassed a considerable fortune. He died on March Bth. 1803, and he will always be remembered as the "father of British inland navigation." It is said that owing to a disappointment in a love affair, the Earl remained un- married, and developed into a misogynist. He left all his property—which consisted for the most part of canals and colleries—in the hands of trustees for a hundred years for the benefit of his grand-nephew, the first Earl Ellesmere. It is suggested that the Earl had another motive in making this strange bequest and that his real object in creating the trust was to secure the advantage of his canals to the public. The value of the property has increased considerably during the last thirty years. The Bridgwater Canal was sold in 1873 for £989,612, and it was transferred again in 1887 to the Manchester Ship Canal Company for £1,710,000. A story was current recently to the effect that as the trust termin- ated on March Bth this year, the Earl of Ellesmere would come into a vast fortune. The Earl,however, has stated that the trust does not terminate until the autumna.nd that when it does it will make no difference to him, because he has received the income from the Bridgwater estates for the past thirty -years. The Earl of Ellesmere is in his fifty-sixth year.

div.head: MEMORIAL.
div.p: THE MEMORIAL.

The Bridgwater Trust was really formed to manage the Earl's estates in Lancashire, but a very fine monu- ment is erected to his memory on the estate which he owned at Ashridge, Hertfordshire. This estate was not included in the trust, but was left to General John William Egerton, from whom it descended to the Cust family. It is now in the possession of the Earl a Brownlow. The monument, which is 200 ft. in height, stands on a hill 500 ft above the sea. From the summit of the hill—which is reached by a flight of stone steps —some of the finest views in Hertfordshire, Bucking- hamshire and Bedfordshire can be obtained. The monument was erected in recognition of the eminent services the Earl had rendered to his country.

div.head: LEAVING WORK WITHOUT NOTICE. Damages Against an Employee at WatTington.
div.p: LEAVING WORK WITHOUT NOTICE. Damages Against an Employee at WatTington.

An unusual case occupied the attention of the magis- trates at the Warrington Police Court on Friday when Thomas Wall, 113, Cartwright-street, was sued by the Whitecross Company, Limited, for £lO loss caused to the firm in !consequence of his leaving work without giving proper notice on March 23rd. Mr. Browne appeared for the company and said he was instructed to recover damages from the defendant for a very serious matter. Defendant was the head roller in number four mill. He had a very important position to fulfil, having no fewer than ten men under him. His duty was to commence work at six o'clock on the Monday evening in question and continue to work until the following morning. Defendant came on duty perfectly Sober at six o'clock. Shortly before 9.30, Mr. Jones, the assistant manager, went round to the mill to see that everything was going right. He found that the work was going on and defendant was there. He went away for about ten minutes and on returning found the defendant had gone away. The whole mill was stopped and Mr. Jones couldnot find the defendant anywhere. He informed Mr. Legge, the manager of the department, of what had occurred, and tried to get a Iman to take defendant's place but could not. The defendant was found at about 10.40 and could not give any reasonable explanation- of his conduct because he was greatly under the influence of drink. The mill had to be closed for the night, and when it came to be reckoned up it was found that the total loss to the firth was £3O lls. 6d. In addition the loss of wages to the men was £4 14s. The magistrates had no jurisdiction in claims for amounts over £lO and therefore it was decided to give defendant credit for £6 19s. 4d wages due to him and to sue for Defendant called at his (Mr, Browne's) office and said he had been aggravated by the workmen, some of whom were under the influence of drink. The work was not going on right and defendant saw that if he had not left the mill and the work had continued most of the stuff would have been spoiled. He offered a sum of £3 or £4 in settlement of the case, but Mr. Carson instructed him (Mr. Browne) not to accept any- thingas he was determined to make an example of the man. The magistrates made RR order for the payment of £lO and costs in the course of a fortnight.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION CUP.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION CUP.
SEMI-FINALS.
SALFORD v. OLDHAM.
These teams- met at Broughton on Saturday before 19,000 spectators. Both sides were fully represented, and a very hard game was the result, the match ending in a pointless draw.

div.head: HALIFAX v. HULL.
div.p: HALIFAX v. HULL.

This match was played on the Huddersfield ground before 18,000 people, who witnessed a fine game. Halifax won the toss, but Hull scored first through Moxon after clever combination. Halifax soon equal- ised, Joe Riley getting a try. Then Bartle scrambled over with another and Wedgwood placed a goal. At half-time Halifax led by eight points to three points. In the second half Hull played well but had no luck. Goddard kicked a penalty goal, and Parry was twice stopped on the line, the result being Halifax eight points, Hull five points.

div.head: LEAGUE.---FIRST DIVISION.
div.p: THE LEAGUE.---FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.

These teams met for the first time this season, at Wigan on Saturday. There had been a lot of rain in the morning, but the afternoon was tine. The ground, however, was in a shocking state, pools of water and inches of mud covering the whole of the playing area. There was some doubt about playing the match, but the referee finally decided in favour of going on with the game. Both sides were representative, and lined-up as follows :

Wigan—Mason, back; Green, Dickinson, A. Duffy, and Rouse, three-quarter backs; Anderson, and Threl- fall, half-backs' Ball, Collier, Topping, H. Duffy, Elli- son, Beesley, Hatton, and Wolfenden, forwards. . Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood,Dicken- son, and Harris, three-quarter backs; Edmunds and Duckworth, half-backs; Boardman, Edmondson, Foster, Jolley, Morrison, Swift, Coleman and Harmer forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford. Touch judges, Mr. T. Radcliffe, Swinton, and Mr. P. Taylor' Leeds. There were five thousand srectators, and Dickenson started for Warrington against the wind. The visitors •were first to attack, Fish being pushed in touch at the corner early on. Warrington hotly assailed the Wigan goal and Dickenson must have scored had not Edmunds pass been short and the ball stuck in the mud. Wigan eventually got clear bylong kicking and up to the inter- val play was even there being no scoring. In the second half Warrington were again seen to advantage in the loose, the three-quarters passing with splendid precision. Wigan, however, were the first to score, Anderson dodging through the thick of the opposing backs after Hallam's kick had been charged down. Mason landed the extra two points. Wigan maintained the lead until close on time, when Foster dribbled over under the posts, Fish registering the goal. Result :—Wigan 1 goal and 1 try (5 points), Warrington 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).
WIDNES V. HUDDERSFIELD: THE REFEREE AND THE SPECTATORS.

Played at Widnes, before 2,000 spectators. Hudders- field won the toss and Aspey otarted against a strong wind. Widnes got their opponents quarter, and a round of passing took place which ended in Bown being pushed into touch at the corner flag. F. Dewhurst, by means of judicious kicking, took play to centre, and the game settled down here for some time. At this stage several decisions of the referee did not meet with the approval of a certain section of the home spectators, and they made their feelings known. The referee (Mr. Farrar) stopped the game, and, walking up to the stand, saidunless the jeering was discontinued he would stop the game altogether. The caution had the desired effect. Rea,dyhough failed to gather the ball, and Hughes, following up, dribbled it over the line and scored a try. Tilley failed at the place. On resuming Huddersfield attacked, and a miss-kick-gave Litrard a chance, and he scored. Sutcliffe failed at goal. Half-time score : Widnes 1 try (3 points), Huddersfield 1 try (3 points). Immediately on re-starting Widnes went away with a rush, and smart play by Bown enabled Tilley who had exchanged places with J. Taylor, to score at the corner, The same player failed at goal. Shortly after kicking off Naylor was injured, and had to retire. Widnes kept up the attack, and as the result of a forward rush Ley- shon scored another try, the kick at goal failing. After this Huddersfield were penned on' their own line, and Rispan, Aspey, and Tilley scored three more tries, while the latter kicked another goal. Just before the whistle blew Readyhough had his shoulder injured, and had to retire. Result :—Widnes 2 goals 6 tries (22 points), Huddesfleld 1 try (3 points.) div.head: ST. HELENS v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.
div.p: ST. HELENS v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

The meeting of these teams at St. Helens aroused interestlinasmuch as neither were 'altogether clear of the probability of relegation to the Second Division next season. There was a good attendance of spectators I Lea started for the home team, but the Hull forwards I early assumed the aggressive, Liversedge easing the pressure. The Hull men were again dangerous, and passing by Barry, Gordon, and West ended in the last- named scoring, but Starks failed at goal. The Saints , next broke away, but Sinclair riiturned the ball, and I once more the defenders were hard pressed. Again some I nice passing was shown by Phillips, Gordon and West., I and the latter scored another unimproved try, and half- time arrived witi the score :—Hull Kingston Rovers 2 tries (6 points), St.. Helens nil.—Tn the second half, with the wind in their favour, the Saints gave a better display. Early on, from a scrummage, Jones gained possession and neatly dropped a goal. The subsequent play was fairly even, but there was no further soorin't. Result : Hull Kingston Rovers 2 tries (6 points), St. Helens 1 goal (2points). Teams:— St. Helens—Wearing, back; C. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The Final Meeting—Vote of Thanks.

The final meeting of the Board for 190 2-3 was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednes- day morning. Dr. Patterson presided and there were also present :—Rev. T. R. Matthews, Rev. Father Wilson, Mrs. Clay, Dr. Murray, Messrs. A. Brooks, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, Cl. Pilling, S. Davies, J. Payton, T. H. Ashcroft, J. Billinge, William Houghton, J. Turton, R. Forshaw, Cl. Mather, T. Halton, W. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), F. Gate (workhouse master).

div.head: ACCEPTANCE OF ADDITIONAL TENDERS.
div.p: ACCEPTANCE OF ADDITIONAL TENDERS.

The tenders referred to the House Coramittee for consideration were now submitted for acceptance as follows: groceries, Messrs. E. Richardson and Son; drapery, Messrs. Cartwright of London; boots and shoes, Messrs. R. Roberts and Son; coal and slack, Messrs. R. Evans and Co., Limited; brushes, Mr. Ratcliffe, Priestley-street. These recommendations were approved. THE CLERK OF THE ASSESSMENT COM-

MITTEE'S SALARY. Mr. PILLING in moving the passing of cheques amounting to £4,275 7s Od. said he would also include in his recommendation that the usual salary of £25 be paid to Mr. Sutton as clerk of the Assessment Com- mittee subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. This course was agreed to. THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE'S EXISTENCE.

The CLERK said he took it from a communication he had received from the ißoard of Education,- that the School Atteedance Committee would continue their services and the officers would continue to act, until Michaelmas next.

div.head: SUPERINTENDENT NURSE.
div.p: THE SUPERINTENDENT NURSE.

The CLERK reported that he had received a communi- cation from the Local Government Board approving of the appointment of Miss M. J.Biggin as superintendent nurse from the Local Government Board. THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Padget() Schools Committee, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman and Vice- chairman for their services daring the past year and also to the superintendent, the matron and staff. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. A. J. Jolley.

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee it was recommended that the flaggmg,paving and asphalting of the yards be oarried out as per the plan submitted by the Master and that he obtain prices for the various kinds of material. Nurse Rodgers having tendered her resigna- tion it was recommended that the Master communicate with Miss Kett asking her to supply another nurse at a salary of £27 10s. with the usual allowances. The Master was instructed to communicate with Mr. Brad- shaw who has been appointed receiver ra the Warring- ton District Electric Light Company and ask for the immediate delivery of the Board's motor switch. The minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. A. Brooks.

div.head: VOTE OF THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.
div.p: VOTE OF THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said he would like to be allowed the privilege of proposing that the best thanks of the Boaid be given to Dii. Patterson for his services in the chair during the past year. As his predecessor in that honorary position he (Mr. Jolley) had some idea of what the duties were. When Dr. Patterson was elected a year ago he promised to do his best and to discharge the duties to the satisfaction of the Board. He (Mr. Jolley) ventured to think that the promise Dr. Patter- son made had been fulfilled. (Hear, hear.) The anticipa- tions of the Board as to how Dr. Patterson would dis- charge the duties had been fully realised. His geniitlity and urbanity—he would not say had won the esteem of all, for they had a warm feeling for him before—but the good feeling which existed before. his appointment to the chair had not been in any way lessened but rather strengthened by his conduct in the chair during the past twelve months. (Hear, hear.) Mr. S. DAVIES said he had great pleasure in second- ing the vote of thanks. The past year had net been a very eventful year of office, for theyhadnot hadthose angry and unnecessary debates which so many of them listened to in the past. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman had therefore been able to get through his duties with comparative ease. They all knew that Dr. Patterson had done his best and he had been most kind and cour- teous to all the members during his term of office. It was as little as they could do to reciproaate that feeling by passing a vote of thanks. - They all felt with the Chairman in the sad bereavement which overtook him during his term of office and he felt sure he was express- ing the feeling of the Board when he said they sym- pathised with him. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. BILLINGS in [supporting the proposition, said the Newton Relief Committee had acquired the happy art of educating good chairmen and he was glad that Dr. Patterson had conducted the business so amicably and peaceably that there had been no need for friction, or any physical force applied to the male or female members of the Board. (Laughter). Dr. Patterson had given great satisfaction and had endeared himself to the hearts of all.

The proposition was put to the meeting by Mr. BROOKS and unanimously carried. The CHAIRMAN, in acknowledging the compliment, said he had done the best he could and he was very proud indeed to have held the high office of chairman. Before he concluded he would like to move a vote of thanks to Mr. Brooks,the senior.vice-chairman who had always been present and when necessarrhad taken his place at interim meetings. He remembered that when he was elected chairm-n a new arrangement was made. Personally he did not know the Warrington poor. He did know the poor of the Newton district and he had pleasure in sitting on the Newton Relief Committee. He had to thank Mr. A. J. Jolley and Mr. Pilling for kindly presiding as Chairmen of the two town relief committees. He understood it Was an arrangement that had acted well and he hoped it would be continued. The thanks of the Board were due to them. (Hear, hear.) _ _

Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON seconded the vote of thanks to the gentlemen named and it was unanimously carried. The CHAIRMAN said he forgot to include the junior vice-chairman (Mr. Knowles). Mr. A. BROOKES, in reply, said his duties as vice- chairman had been only nominal.

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said he appreciated very highly the expressions of the Chairman. For many years he (Mr. Jolley)had taken a keen interest in the administration of relief. The work had been made easier by the support he had received from the Guardians who had made a point of attending the relief committees. Mr. PILLING said he was very much obliged for the vote of thanks. The Bohrd then rose.

SIR WILLI A3l ANOTHER ATTACK ON ANSON'S explanation POPULAR EDUCATION, of the Government

Bill for the destruc- tion of the London School Board was received on one side of the House of Commons with much derisive laughter, and on the other with some grave doubt of its practicability. It is actually a much worse Bill than anybody expected the Government to produce. It exceeds, as Sir HENRY CAMPBELL BANNERMAN said, the worst fears of those who are anxious for an effective and per- manent solution of the education problem. The condemnation passed on it by Dr. MACNAMARA
was not less complete. The Bill is so bad, he 'sap, that the House will not find it possible to tinker

with in. Sir WILLIAM Amor is more of a University Don than a practical statesman, and he revealed the real purpose of himself and his celleagues—W-iih what hispolitical chief must have considered to be an indiscreet !thorough- ness. He delivered, as the Liberal leader re- marked, a homily against representative govern- ment. There has been nothing like it since the Reform Bill, Sir Ef EN. RY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN declared. The early portion of his speech abounded in such surprising statements as that a popularly elected vbody tends to over-centralisation ; that it necessarily and inevitably becomes an extravagant body and so on. Therefore the London School Board must go. "A great variety of interest "his to be substituted for a directly representative authority. The London School Board,he said,hae placed under immense obligation the parents and children of London. He could only hope that the management under his own system would be as efficient as that of the School Board had been. It is a body of which things like this can be said, without feeling and sincerity, that the Govern- ment is guilty of the almost incredible folly of wighing to destroy.

The London County Council is nominally to be the education authority under the new Bill. But not more than nominally, for even Sir WILLIAM ANSON is not able to say more than that "to a great extent" it will be placed in the posi- tion in which the provincial Councils were placed by the Act of last year. The County Council will havA the rating power for schools, but very little else. Sir WILLIAM ANSON simply creates chaos. Having declared the County Council to be Gbe education authority he proceeds to explain thap the Borough Councilb are to have the manage- ment of the schools. This is what he calls decen- tralisation. It will, in practice, result in the setting up of i% different system in everY borough in London. The Borough Councils ere to have the appointment and dismissal of teacher* but not, of course, in the so-called volunte,/

achnele, which are to be placed under the provis- i°ne of the Act of last year. They are, that is t ) say, to be placed on the rates, and to be managed by the parsons under a system which imposes a zeligious test on teachers. Then, having joined the London County Council and the Borough 'Councils in a manner whim will produce perpetual 'conflict, the Government Bill goes on to cemstitute a marvellously composite committee. This, Sir WILLIAM Arrsorr explains, is by way of giving 'ft the fullest assistance to the County Council." leeh borough is to send one representative to the committee. The city of London and the city of'Westminster each send two. Bodies so nnlike each other as the London University, the parochial charities, and the city guilds are to rePresented. Five members are to be selected 'from the London School Board to hold office for 4e years. 'The London City Council is to be Permitted to contribute 36 members out of close Oe a hundred.; and that is What the Government calla making: the County Council the education authority! Sir Jourr GORST had the eftrontery to describe this extraordinary-scheme as democra- tic) and Sir WILLIAM ANSON spoke of 62 of the embers of the committee as being the result of election." They are the 'result of election, no doubt, but of election to other bodies existing for other ends ancl not to this committee, which!is to be entrusted .91itil the administration for education purposes of revenue equal to that of some ',European States. might have been possible to construct a good .w'uenle, even whilst destroying the education eethority which has a reclid of th;rty years of ,4rairable work behind it. But such is the frantic flatted of this Government of the London County Council, of the London School Board, and, as it ould appear, of the principle of direct popular tvPresentation, that it has produced a scheme ithich is already a laughing stock, and which, should it pass into law, will inevitably throw the nduoational system of London into inextricable and most harmful confusion. " The Cause of earthquakes," said John Wesley, "is sin." How he reasoned it out is not easy for the average sinner to see. The idea of such a tremendous Physical convulsionas an earthquake resulting from the violation of moral law is nonsense in the eyes of modern science. The reverse is more often true. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.

At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, on Monday, Nellie Done (33), married woman, was charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide at Runcorn, on the Ist January. Mr. Colt-Williams, who prosecuted, said it was an ex- ceedingly sad case. Prisoner was a married woman with eight children, and on New Year's Day she was seen seated on the canal bank with a bundle in her arms. She jumped into the water, and was gallantly rescued by a telegraph clerk named Harrison and another man named Ellis. The bundle was found to contain a child, which was also rescued. The doctor had been attending the poor woman for hysteria and insomnia. Prisoner was bound over.

!SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. On Tuesday a shocking accident befel Mr. William Rushton, aged seventy-three years of age, of Greenway road, Runcorn. Mr. Rushton is a cooper at the local works of the United Alkali Company, and he was in a disused building, when a considerable portion of the outer wall, nine inches thick fell, and he was buried in the debris. Aid was at hand, and he was quickly un- covered. From the position of his body it appeared as though the unfortunate man had been stooping to pick up something. He was conveyed home on a stretcher, and attended to by Dr. IVl'Dougall and Dr. M'Lennan. His injuries are very severe. His head is badly cut, his right leg is fractured at the thigh, and the foot of his right leg is so badly smashed that amputation will be necessary. He has also sustained some internal injury.

div.head: ESTIMATES.
div.p: THE ESTIMATES.

The estimated expenditure for 1903-4, is £9,954; the estimated income is £1,560, with a balance of £4BO in the treasurer's hands, making a total of £2,040. The difference between expenditure and income is therefore £7,914, the amount to be provided from the rates. A penny in the £ produces £lBB, so that 3s. 6d. in the I producing £7,896, will be required. Mr. Imison proposed the adoption of the foregoing estimates.'He said it would be a relief to the ratepayers to know that the Council did not find it necessary to levy an increased rate. The anticipations of last year had been fulfilled. They had met all the obligations and also the special proceedings connected with the coronation proceedings. A satisfactory feature was that the productiveness of the penny rate had increased by £4 from £lB4 to £lBB—and as they raised altogether forty two pennies, it meant that the rate had realised £l6B more than had been anticipated. This showed that property hitherto unoccupied had been used. He moved that the general district rate be 3s. 6d. in the Z. Mr. Handley seconded and the estimates were ap- proved.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION CUP.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION CUP.
SALFORD v, OLDHAM. THE RE-PLAY-SALFORD WIN.

Salford and Oldhaun played on Wednesday, at Brough- ton, their tie in the semi-final for the Northern Union. Cup, and Salford won well by eight points to nothing. The victory ought to have been more substantial, but the place-kicking was valueless, and as a consequence neither of Salford's tries was improved upon. The first try was obtained before the game was many minutes old by the Salford captain, Lomas. After the interval the difference between the teams became more emphasised, and long before the finish hawkers were gathering pennies for cards announcing the" fatal fall of Oldham.'" Griffiths, close under the bar, dropped a capital goal. Afterwardsthe Salford right wing made an opening and from the succeeding scrummage Norris got over the line. Salford's superiority was very decided both in attack and defence, and L omas's work, save for his place-kicking, was exceptionally brilliant,. Salford will *ow meet Halifax in the final, which will be played at Leeds on April 25.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

At last Mr. G. F. Clarke has secured a seat on the District Council. This was his fourth attempt, and by a majority of 40 votes he succeeded in defeating Mr. A. Evett for the Crow-lane Ward. Varying interests were at work, and late on Saturday night a pamphlet, any- thing but complimentary to Mr. Clarke, was circulated at every house in the Ward. One of Mr. Clarke's elec- tion placards stated "Vote for Clarke, who resides in the Ward." Certainly he resides in the Ward, bilt he is only present in it for a few hours each night. His busi- ness calls him away from Earlestown all the day, and howhe can possiblyacquaiut himself with thenecessities of the township, is beyond comprehension. He may be gifted with second sight, but he cannot by any means be in two places at one time. However' thin will show how he is able to fulfil his promise of doing his duty to the ratepayers.

People are beginning to wonder whit the intentions of the committee are, which WAS elected to deal with the funds which were subscribed nearly three years ago for the relief of sufferers by the late war. It is known that there is a balance of something like £BOO still in the bank, and it is the disposal of this sum which troubles many. It Wt 1.43 said some time ago that there was an intention to erect some kind of memorial to the local soldiers and volunteers who had fallen in the war, and those who had given their services and returned un- injured. This, there is no objecti4on to but there may be trouble as to the disposal of the balance.

Now the movement for a cottage hospital is one which cannot be 'overlooked, for in spite of the opposi- tion which prevails in SOM3 quarters, the project will be carried through sooner or later. If the balance from the war fund, after providing for the memorial, was devoted to the hospital fund, it' would, I am sure, meet with the approval of the subscribers, and the committee would be well advised to vote it for this worthy local object.-

div.head: ST. PETER'S BIBLE CLASS, NEWTON.
div.p: ST. PETER'S BIBLE CLASS, NEWTON.

On Saturday the members of this Bible Class to the number of about 50 accompanied by the Rev. James Ryder, vicar,had a pleasant and interesting outing. Per- mission had been obtained for the party to view the White Star steamer Cedric which was lying in the Canada Dock at Liverpool, and leaving Newton about one o'clock, they reached the vessel about half-past two, by means of the overhead railway. An exhaustive inspection of the steamer was made and everybody was highly delighted. The party afterwards crossed the river to New Brighton where they had tea. The out was thoroughly enjoyed, the enjoyment being enhanced by the fine weather.

div.head: AN ALLEGED NUISANCE.
div.p: AN ALLEGED NUISANCE.

Mr. W. H. Woodcock, of Warrington wrote on March 25th, calling attention to a nuisance which existed in the lane leading from Mr. Darbyshire's farm toward theWatemorks Reservoir. It seemed to him that the drainage from the farm ran into the open ditch by the side of the road and produced an intolerable stench which must be very detrimental to health. Unless removed it certainly would detract from one of the pleasantest walks. Inspector Farrington said he had visited the place and had ascertained that at this period of the year the ditchlby the road side was in its worst condition,owing to a local farmer letting hir refuse run into the ditch. The farmer had promised to clear the ditch and he thought this would remedy the nuisance. WESTON WATER. AN IMPORTANT 'MOVE.

Mr. E. Marshall wrote for the Runcorn Urban Dis- trict Council under date March 31st. :—" Dear Sir,—ln reply to your letter of 25th, with regard to the water supply to cottages, Beaconsfleld-view and Clarke's- terrace, Weston Point, I may say that the last letter I addressed to you on this matter was read to my Water Committee, and was approved by them. The Salt Union have applied to my Council for the supply of a large vantity of water for their Mond Gas plant. In all probability a larger main will be needed than the one now in to enable us to give the requisite supply. if this is done it will meet, the wishes of the owners in question, although we feel confident that if a new main is laid the so vice pipes will still be found to be quite inadequate. The Clerk said that some ten weeks ago the Rural Council asked the Urban Council to state the price they required for the water mains in the parishes of Halton and Weston, as the waterwas not. satisfactory. Several letters had been written to the Urban Council, but prac- tically no answer had been given, and they had not attempted to state a price. He would now ask the Rural Council to apply to the Urban Council under the powers of the Private Acts to name an arbitrator whom they wished to appoint to fix the price for the considera- tion of the Rural Council—,the name chosen to be sub- mitted to the Rural District Council. This course of action was agreed upon on the motion of Messrs. Wright and Woodward.
