div.head: A-PARISH COUNCIL PROTEST.
div.p: A-PARISH COUNCIL PROTEST.

Under date April 2nd, Mr. S. J. Woodcock, clerk to the Grappenhall Parish Council wrote notifying the Council that at a meeting of the Parish Council held on March 31st he was directed to write protesting against the expenditure of the Rural District Council re the alleged nuisance at Thelwall being placed as a special expenses charge. The Council considered that it ought to be charged against the highways account. Dr. Vascher's report said "The public road will be widened and ex- tend over the sewer." This was a distinct road improve- ment and should be charged as such. Resolved that the allocation of cost be referred to a committee. DR. WOOD WRITES A SARCASTIC LETTER. _ _

_ Dr. Wood wrote from the Liverpool Sanatorium at Kingswood, stating that he had removed the seats according to the request of the Council. He inferred that the Council laid claim to the road right up to the pricks whereas he was of the opinion that the ' road proper only came to within three feet of the hedge roots. He was sure the Council had refused his applica- tions'only from a strict sense of duty,and that they bore no feeling iof towards the sanatorium and its patients. He would not .be compelled to follow the clever suggestion of Mr. Horton and provide camp stools for the patients. He merely threw that outs»; a suggestion—but was it too much for them to hope that the councillors and especially the members who had opposed his seats so sternly would send a liberal dona- tion towards the camp stools. It would be signal proof that their differences of opinion were caused by no personal feelings and that good feeling still existed.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby 0-Cabal By " Ovalist."
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby 0-Cabal By " Ovalist."

Have you ever been. to Central Park, Wigan, the headquarters of the Wigan Rugby P. 0.? If you have not, take the first opp;tunity of going. It is one of charming charmin sylvan retreats which seem almost profaned by the rude game of football. The " Park " is encircled by low, richly-wooded hills, with grassy slopes of a verdant green, while in the valley lies the football ground, half-encircled by a pellucid stream from the hills beyond. In the eye of the Wiganer, i Central Park is all this and much more. It s the beauteous home of a classic club Playing "classy " football. But what do visitors to the" Park," and particularly Warrington visitors, think of it? Imagination fails me, or I would endeavour to inter- pret their thought,Thut I dare not, for the credit of this respectable family newspaper, put into cold type some of the things they said. Suffice it to describe my own experiences.

On our arrival at Wigan we—that is myself and others—comm.enced a oareful search for Central Park. We had no notion where it was, but presumed that, being a Park, it would not b 3 diffictilt to distinguish from the brick and mortary parts of Wigan. The stalwart figure of the Warrington Club Secretary was espied in front, and with him as a guide we expected to be very sion seated" on the benches in the Park" —listening to the band, maybe, and generally taking it easy " neath the shade of the sheltering palm" what time the players equipped themselves for the fray. Mr. Ashton led the way with unerring accuracy, and in the space of some ten minutes or more we reached the "Park." Yes, there could be no doubt ahput it, for painted boldly on a hoarding which stretched across a tin-can and clinker tip on the left were the magic words : "Central Park. Head- quarters Wigan R.F.C." " Hurrah ! " we should have said, but it stuck in our throats. This a Park, well--!

By and by we got on the ground—there wasn't much, but we got. on it for safety—and surveyed the playing arena. Doubts assailed us. Could this be the football patch or was it the 'Corporation settling tank? There appeared to be nothing but a dangerous-looking expanse of sludge and water surrounded by •a fence which might quite conceivably have been put up to ensure the safety of the public. On it—or in it I should say—were a number of clay-coloured individuals armed with various instruments designed to effectively mix the ingredients, which they proceeded to do. There was something, however, which prevented the water commingling with the rest of the mixture and despite any amount of coaxing the pools remained. Presently the head-mixer waded out and approached us. We queried anxiously "is this really the football ground, or a bacteria bed ? " "Certainly it is," said he, charmingly indefinite, " what's wrong wi' it ? " We murmured that "it might be perfect—for the bacteria." "It's only a bit soft, a bit 'oldin' " said he, and we relapsed into silence with the conviction that this dismal looking sludge-pit really was the football field and Central Park combined.

Mr. Secretary Ashton, usually so urbane and good- tempered, was manifestly wrath. "Impossible to play," he remarked. "Never saw • such a sanguinary swamp in my life" growled another committeeman, while Yet another plunged into the morass and _roamed round in an ecstacy of rage. By and by Wigan officials began to arrive and attempted to quell the storm. "Right enough," "not so bad as it looks" were stock remarks, but eventually Referee Priestley was appealed to. At first it was thought he would postpone the match, but the Wiganers had cutely opened the gates and the crowd backed their appeal's with vociferous exhortations. ,This turned the scale, and the match commenced. One 'cannot say much about it. Up to half time both sides had done a lot of wallowing, but there was no score. Warrington had even played the passing game with some success, but the men's feet were like lead on such a surface and the result was not tangible. In the second half play was rather better, both teams skipping along at a good pace now and then. But of what advantage were skill and cleverness under such conditions? The 'Warrington backs were terribly handicapped, and, though superior to the Wigan lot, they could not get through. Fish ran down to the corner on three occasions, but he could no more double and turn than fly. :Each side eventually got a flukey 5 points and the game ended in a draw. •

There is no question in my mind that the State of the ground robbed Warrington of -victory. It • was evident from the way the backs performed that, on a firm surface, they would have made rings round , the Wiganers, whose ideas of combinatioa were very crude. By halving thcpoints Warrington have, in all probability, lost all chance of the South-West Lanca- shire Cup, and to do so under such conditions is par- ticularly annoying. The Wigan officials are very much to blame in not giving some intimation of the state of the ground in the morning. Farther than this if they cannot provide a better playing surface than that of Saturday the ground ought to be suspen- ded. It is not fit for its intended purpose, and the Northern Union should insist on a certain standard of fitness being attained all rlund. Fortunately for Wigan their case is except ioital, or we should soon have legislation on the subject.

There is not much to be. said of in lividuil pe.rfor.n- ances. On the home side . Anderwm played a fine game at half back,and is a most promising player after the style of Lomas. His efforts were poorly supported however. Mason, the _Wigan full back, also gave a capital exhibition and was considerably ahead of Hallam. it is rather c-ar:ortS that a mistake by each full back should have resulted in the oppo sing side's score. Hallam had his kick charged down, and Mason missed a pass back from one of .his centres, with the result that the energetic Forster dribbled over and scored.

As my readers are aware Warrington had to win at Wigan in order to have a Chance of equalling Run- corn's record in the South West Lancashire Competi- tion, and by failing to get the maximum points the cup will probably go to Runcorn. The latter club have only another match, and this also is against Wigan,but as it takes place on the irwell-lane enclosure there is not much hope for Warrington.
The positions of the clubs in the South-West Lancashire League table now stand as follows :-- Points. P. W. L. D. For Agst. Pts Runcorn 9 ... 5 1 ... 3 ... 61— 7 ...13
The League table up-to-date is as follows : For Agst.

The semi-finals last Saturday were productive of very keen struggles.. Halifax came up to expecta- sions by beating Hull by 8 points to 5 points, but their superiority was so trifling that it is doubtful if they could repeat the performance. Salford and Oldham. fought fruitlessly at Broughton, where there was no scoring. Oldham were even 'thought to have had the better of the game, but the notion that they might enter the final was knocked on the head •on Wednes- day when Salford won by a clear 8 'points to nil and were markedly superior. I never thought Oldham had much chance after seeing. them play Warrington at Watersheddings: They §adly lacked dash iu the rear division, whereas this in Salford's strong point. My prediction for the finalist has worked out cor- rectly, and I still pin my faith to the "Reds." They should account for Halifax on the 25th at Leeds, though they will meet a. team very similar in many respects.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

AI the last meeting of the, committee of the War- rington Anglers' Association fifteen new members were enrolled. It was decided to admit lady mem- bers at an annual subscription of 2s. 6d.; this to in-

elude a travelling card. It was announced that the fishing in the Acker's Pits and Plinston's Pool had been acquired, for the Society. Much satisfaction was expressed when it was made known that the Bridgwater Canal will be available to anglers of Warrington and district ander certain conditions. The question of re- organising the Society was introduced and after a long and keen discussion it was decided to again bring up the matter at the • next meeting of the committee, when probably the matter will be settled in a way that all anglers in the district may participate in the privileges at the disposal of4the society. For the guidance of inexperienced trout fishers this Easter, who may happen to fish rivers where salmon fry abound and to take which is an offence under the fishery laws, the following hints may prove useful. In salmon fry, there are no spots below the medial line, except two or three on the gills, and immediately behind the same. In river trout, there are spots on the dorsal fin, but none on that of the salmon. The fins of salmon are mostly of a light slate colour, but the adipose fin of the river trout is tinged with pink or red, but this is not so with the salmon. There is a white bar dr line on the first ray of the anal fin of the river trout. It is to be hoped that the weather may be all that the angler may de- sire during the Easter recess.

div.head: FOREIGN MISSIONS. Anniversary Services at Bold Street.
div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONS. Anniversary Services at Bold Street.

During the past week, services and lectures have been held in Bold-street Wesley-an Church and school in con- nection with the Foreign Missionary Anniversary. The first service was held on Sunday morning in the church when the Rev. R. Wilkins Rues conducted And delivered an appropriate discourse. The choir, under the conduc- torship of Mr. P. Hickman gave an effective rendering of the anthem" Send out thy Light "(Gounod). The preacher at the evening service was the Rev. G. H. Carnson (superintendent of the circuit) and the anthem "How lovely are the messengers " was sung. There was a large attendance in the schoolroom in the after- noon when an address was delivered to the scholars and friends by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. Special music was rendered by the Male Voice Chorus. The prizes were distributed to the juvenile collections (boys and girls) by Mrs. Neville, and the report of the Secretary (Mr. Geo. Ashton),which was a satisfactary one was read and showed an increase of £lO on the year. Collections were taken up at all the services on behalf of the Wes- leyan Foreign Missionary Society. LECTURE ON THE PROBLEM OF MISSIONS IN INDIA.

There was but a sm-al attendance in the schoolroom on Monday evening when the Rev. James Lewis, of Liverpool, delivered an intensely interesting leaure on "The Church's Problem in India." The chair was

occupied by Councillor James Evans, and he was accom- panied on the platform by the lecturer and the Revs. 0. H. Carnson, (superintendent), and W. C. J. Neville. in the course of a few introductory remarks' the Chairman said he regretted that more people in War- rington did not take an interest in that kind of thing. He was afraid that the old Gospel had not the same charm for people to-day as it had in years gone by. There was more religious freedom to-day and he believed that if an attempt were made to deprive us of some of the advantages we enjoyed it would have the beneficial effect of making us more earnest in the cause of Christ than many were at present. He could not help being struck at the spectacle which was witnessed nightly of thousands crowding into theatres and the sparse con- gregations in the churches. Whilst thousands paid a shilling to witless a performance in a theatre it was difficult to get them into the churches for an ordinary collection. (Laughter.) The Rev JAMES LEWIS, in referring to the chair- man's remarks, said that when they as professing , Christians meant business they would get their churches ' filled once more. (Hear, hear) There was a spirit of apathy and indifference amongst professing Christians for church work which must be removed if the church was to fulfil her work. Proceeding with his lecture on the problems of missions in India, he said that India politically belonged to us English Chris- tians. It was our greatest dependency, it was one of our greatest markets, and we were blest not only materially by India but in other ways. Reference was made to the work which had already been done on behalf of the British Empire by the Indian troops, during the South African campaignand the disturbances in China. We exploited India for our mercantile bene- fit but the arrangements existing between man and man were not purely mercantile, There were other obliga- tions and of a more onerous character, and the burden which was cast upon the British people for the uplifting of the poople of India was greater than many conceived We were apt to speak of the people of India as natives and niggers, but he would remind them that India was a highly civilised nation in the days when our forefathers were savages. Five hundred years before Christ's time they had their system of Buddhism, land Christianity had been in India almost as lon as it had been in England. in the sixth century, the Syrian church was established on the West coast of India, but it had no power of growth or development in it. The Christians of St. Thomas in India were known to King Alfred who sent two ambassadors to them bearing pre- sents. The reformation in Europe had tremendous con- sequences for India, for it resulted in the first mission- aries being sent out to India by the Jesuits. As the result of Roman Catholic work in India there are now close upon two millions of Catholics in India. Refer- ence was made to the Danish missionaries to India of the 17th century and the Dutch missionaries a little later to Ceylon. Coming to the close of the 18th century, he said England began to take an interest in missionaryl effort and the first English missionary to Indiavvas a cob bier named William Carey. The interest of Wesleyans in India was aroused by Dr. Coke who died on his way out and was buried in the Indian ocean. There were now about one million Protestants in India to-day. The increase of the Christian population in India during the past ten years had beenlabnormal, and Catholics and Protestants numbered 2,900,000. They would under- stand the magnitude of the problera better when he told them that the population was 294,000,000, but the Christians knew they had truth on their side and were convinced that India would eventually be converted to Christianity. The lecturer said the highly civilised -peoples of India presented a very difficult problem. A member of a high caste family who embraced Christianity was thereby divorced from his wife; his conjugal rights were absolutely destroyed ; he ceased to have any rights to his own children; he was deprived of his property and be suffered social astrocism. The lecturer referred to the privacy of the family altar in India and said the home in India was the Sanctuaryand holy place to which none but the members of the family were admitted. One of the most amazing mistakes made by the Government during the recent plague was the forcing of the low caste into the homes of the Hindoos for the purpose of whitewashing and other purposes. If that practice had not been stopped im- mediately we should have had a storm in India that we could not quell. There were two millions of educated Hindoos in the civil service of India and only 70,000 British soldiers. We could not hold India n day if the Hiudoos did not believe in our justice and mercy and honesty. The Lecturer pointed out that there were many Hindoos who were on the brink of Christianity but who were not prepared at present to make the great sacrifices which a confession of the Christian faith in- volved. India presented problems for the ruler' for the politician and for the Christian Church. The lecturer paid a tribute to the great services which England had rendered to India. and stated that the hearts of the people were warming towards Christianity. He appealed for more generous help for the missionaries of India who were working with great success, despite many difficulties.
The meeting terminated with an acknowledgment of the lecturer's services on the proposition of the Rev. G. H. Canison.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.

The election fora representative for Crow-lane Ward on the District Council in the room of Mr. J. Fitzgerald took place on Monday. The candidates were Mr. G. F. Clarke and Mr. A. Evett and plenty of mural literature was circulated. Considerable interest was taken in the contest and plenty of vehicles were requisitioned in- cluding a motor cycle. The polling Oat:on was at the Wesleyan schools and the counting was carried out at the Town Hall. Mr. C. Cole, Clerk to the Council,was returning officer. At 20 minutes to 9 the result was announced to the large crowd which had gathered in front of the Town Hall, as follows: CLARKE EVETT l9B
Majority for Clarke A vote of thanks to Mr. Cole and the officials was accorded on the motion of Mr. Clarke, seconded by Mr. Evett. _ _ _

_ On the balcony Mr. Clarke said he was glad to have the opportunity of thanking the ladies and gentlemen electors of Crowlane ward for having returned him by a majority of 40 votes, and he could only say that he should endeavour to do his duty as a member of the Urban District Council and to see that the ratepayers of Crow lane ward had not believed all the scurrilous lies that had been"! circulated against himself, in the local press, which was not worth 'my consideration. he could only say, the local press notwithstanding, he should endeavour tb do his duty. (Cheers.) Mr. Evett also addressed the crowd thanking all those who had voted for him, and should occasion arise again he hoped the issue would be different to what it was that night. (Cheers.)

div.head: DREDGING OF THE MERSEY.
div.p: THE DREDGING OF THE MERSEY.
WARRINGTON TRADERS WIN.
JUDGMENT AGAINST THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
Tolls to be Refunded and Damages Paid.

On Tuesday Mr. Justice Byrne delivered, in the Chancery Division, his reserved judgment in the case brought by Messrs. Crostleld and Sons, two other limited liability companies, and the Corporation of Warrington, to enforce their claims against the Man- chester Ship Canal Company on the ground that the Canal Company had failed to dredge the Mersey at Warrington to the extent required by their Acts. His Lordship said the relief claimed by the Corporation and by their co-plaintiffs in their respective capacity was for declarations to establish alleged rights, while the traders individually claimed repayment of canal tolls paid by them under protest, which they alleged to have been wrongfully exacted from them, and, as a separate matter, damages for delay occasioned by neglect to preserve a channel in a portion of the river Mersey in accordance with statutory obligations imposed on the defendants. The case raised important questions of construction arising out of the Manchester Ship Canal Acts, 1885 and 1896, and the terms of an agreement scheduled to the later Act.

div.head: COLLECTIVE AND SEPARATE RIGHTS.
div.p: COLLECTIVE AND SEPARATE RIGHTS.

He was quite clear that some of the sub-sections of the Acts conferred rights on the Corporation only and others upon traders, manufacturers, and others carrying on business at or near Warrington directly. It appeared to him that certain of the sub-sections imposed oblig:t- tions on the Company towards all ithose for whose pro- tection the section was enacted, and notably he con- sidered that sub-section 14 conferred a direct right upon and gave a right of action to all or any of the per- sons mentioned for whose protection the section was introduced. Thcsdredging of the Mersey required to be done by the Company could not be completed by the 31st December, 1893, and in consideration of the Cor- poration consenting not to oppose the opening of the canal on the Ist January, 1894, the Company bound themselves effectually to complete at their own cost the dredging authorised by section 88 on or before the Ist July, 1891, and for every day on which the Company should be in default in respect of the completion of the dredging the Company undertook to forfeit and pay to the Corporation £5O per day as liquidated damages. After the canal was opened disputes arose between the Corporation and the Company in connection with the , dredging of the Mersey at Warrington, especially with regard to the dimensions of the channel. On the 9th 'April, 1896, a new agreement was entered into between the Corporatioh and the Company. He had to construe , the words of clause 7 of the agreement as though it were a statutory enactment in the local and personal Act of 1885 in order to determine the first question at issue between the parties. Th his judgment the words were
CLEAR AND UNAMBIGUOUS

and thereby a duty was imposed upon the Company forthwith to dredge a channel in the river having a minimum width of 50ft. at the bottom and thencefor- ward to maintain a channel of the like minimum width, so that at all times there should be a depth of Bft. of water at low water of spring tides in the channel between the western boundary of the works of Monks, Hall and Co., at or near Bank Quay and Howley Lock, including the portion of the old bed of the Mersey between the westerly end of the river diversion and Howley Lock. Theicont9ntion on behalf of the Canal Company was that their obligation as to dredging was to be measured not by the actual depth of water at low water of spring tides but by an arbitrary fixed level of 10ft. above ordnance datum, so that if the channel were dredged to a depth of Bft. below this level it was sutfi- cleat, even though the result was that there was only 7ft. 6in. or sft. of water. He thought there was no justification for the Canal Company's contention. What the Corporation and traders of Warrington wanted was an actual depth of water to float their vessels, and this was what the Legislature intended to secure for them, and the obligation imposed on the Canal Company could not be answered by dredging so as to give ift. Gin. or sft. of water plus so much air or mud as would make up the Bft. He thought, therefore, that the -Corporation and the traders, suing in their representative capacity, were entitled to a proper declaration in respect of this head of relief claimed. The next question was whether or not in fact the Canal Company had since the passing of the Act of 1896 fulfilled their statutory obligation, first as from the date of the agreement of forthwith dredging a channel of the minimum width and depth defined by the substituted sub-section 14 of section 88, and, secondly. of maintaining the same width and depth. He was clearly of opinion that
THE CANAL COMPANY HAD FAILED TO FULFIL THEIR

OBUGATIONS. He thought that the statutory channel had never been maintained. He was of opinion that the traders in their representative capacity were entitled to a declaration establishing their rights accordingly. He had no doubt that the plaintiff traders as individuals were respectively entitled to recover such moneys paid for tolls wrong- fully demanded and paid under protest. He therefore proposed to direct an inquiry to ascertain the amount of such payments. He thought that the Canal Company were liable to the individual plaintiffs for damages I suffered by them by reason of their neglect to keep the channel dredged in accordance with their obligations. There was sufficient evidence of some damage, and an inquiry should go. He could appreciate the difficulties the Canal Company had had and would have to contend with in fulfilling their statutory obligations, but he had to deal with them as they existed. He was satisfied that there was no impossibility in fulfilling them. He rejected altogether the arguments founded upon the suggestion that as the Act contemplated continuous dredging therefore there need never be a complete channel of the statutory depth and width. If in order to secure ft channel at all times at low Iriter of spring tides of the proper dimensions the dredging Must be io conducted as to make a deeper channel at the time of actual dredging than the statutory one, it must be done: If one dredger was not enough two or more must be employed, and if the 'present ground for depositing the results of the dredging on was not sufficient other ground must be provided, or dredged material must be other- wise disposed of. The normal condition of the channel must in his opinion, be such as to give the statutory width of channel and depth of water, and the necessity for giving notice.s to remove obstructions ought only to be required under abnormal circumstances.
WHAT THE COMPANY MUST DO.

Mr. Justice Byrne then said he would make a declara- tion that the defendant Company were bound at their own cost to Maintain dredged the bed and the banks of the Mersey between the western boundary of Monks, Hall, and •Co. at or near Bank Quay and Howley Lock, including the old portion of the bed of the 'Mersey be- tween the westerly end of the river diversion and Walton Lock to the width of 50 feet, so that at all times there should be a depth of eight feet between the boundaries His Lordship declared that the eight feet meant eight feet of water below the low water level of 'Spring tides and not eight feet below the permanent datum line,and the Court, being of opinion that the defendants since the 16th August, 1899, had failed to maintain such channel, and that navigation had always since that date been obstructed, and that the defendants had not on receipt of written notice from the Warrington surveyor dredged thechannel to the satisfaction of the surveyor declared that from the 16th August, 1899, to the present time the traders, manufacturers, and others darrying on business at or near Warrington, including the plaintiffs were entitled to the right of navigation in respect of vessels passing through the Manchester Ship Canal. He must also declare that the traders, as from the 16th August, 1898,were entitled to recover from the defend- ants all tolls and dues paid by them respectively to the defendants under protest, which, in accordance with the last declaration, the defendants were not entitled to charge. He would grant ap inquiry as to what wai the amount so found to be repaid with interest at 4 per cent, and he would declare that the traders, &c were entitled to recover damages for injury caused by a breach of the defendants' obligations to maintain dredged the channel in question, regard being had to the 'tact that the plaintiffs did not claim damages before the Ist January, 1900. Mr. Bousfleld, for the plaintiffs, said he and Mr. Cripps thought thatthere must be some discussion as to costs and documents, and heasked his Lordship to give them a day next sittings on which they could mention the case.

Mr.iCripps said the questions with regard to the documents would take some time in discussion. Mr. Justice Byrne thought that the plaintiff's junior counsel could draft the minutes on the lines he had suggested, and submit them to Mr. Clare, for the defen- dants, and the matter could be mentioned on the points on which the parties were not agreed. Mr. Bousfield said the plaintiffs might have a sugges- tion to make on the point as to how the inquiry as to damages should be conducted. Mr. Justice Byrne: Fight it out between yourselves, and reduce it to a small number of points ; but if T find you are opening up a wide field I shall cut you very short. The costs generally the plaintiffs are entitled to.
Mr. Flonsfield : On the higher scale ? Mr. Justice Byrne: Most certainly not. There has been a great deal of extravagance in the preparation of this case.
The Ship Canal Company have decided to appeal against this decision, and notice of appeal will be served immediately.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must malt cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as .a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances undertake to return the manuscripts which are not used.
MIEM

div.head: Suggested Incorporation of Stockton- Heath with Warrington.
div.p: Suggested Incorporation of Stockton- Heath with Warrington.

Sir.—With your permission, I should like to be al- lowed to supplement my last Saturday's letter, by seine observations covering a few of the queries that have, since, been personally made to me ; and which queries may probably have occurred to other of your readers with whom I have not had the privilege of conversing., First,l ought to explain that the idea of incorporating Stockton Heath with Warrington was an accidental or secondary suggestion in my last week's letter, and was introduced by me, more as bearing upon "ways and means" for my primary suggestion as to the ad- visability of looking thoughtfully and thriftily ahead, in the direction of providing a suitable Cantilever high- level bridge, over the Ship Canal, at Stockton Heath. However as this incidental topic has- attracted public attention. I will endeavour to open-out some further details or side-lights : (1) As a separate community, keeping selfishly, (let us be frank in the matter) apart from the political and municipal life of Warrington, Stockton Heath can only deserve and expect to remain in its present stunted, stagnant, isolated, inglorious Parish Council or local. vestry sort of existence. (2) lam quite open to correction,and hope that I ani mistaken, but if my information is correct, then the sanitation or sewage system of Stockton Heath is in a condition that needs technical grasp, and an early expenditure, that only Warrington Corporation could successfully deal with. To those who doubt my state- ment, I will only ask one question (and lapin say that, as a resident of Stockton Heath, I hope I inn mistaken) are there cess-pools in Stockton Heath, for the draining of the water-closets? If I am wrongly informed, willingly apologise beforehand to the Parish Council,. and I await official contradiction. If I am rightly. informed, then, every intelligent man or woman in Stockton Heath should help to bring incorporationwith Warrington speedily, or we may—by and by—have an epidemic of diphtheria and fever. Instead of paying a trifle, in the form of municipal rates, we may be called upon to pay a priceless tax of valuable lives! Our local selfishness will inevitably bring its own Nemesis, for there is no social danger so certain, so sudden, and so terribly fatal as a bad system of drainage. A hot, summer, or a damp,hu mid, autumn may bring an out- break of disease which would be very difficult to light, under existing sanitary conditicns. It must not be thought that the undoubtedly pure air of Stockton Heath is any real antidote or panacea against the many diseases arising from bad drainage, for I had a sharp experience of my own, in early youth, bearing upon this very point. 1: , lived in a mountain village, but the population had out- grown the sanitary system; and with the result that not scores but hundreds (including myself) were attacked with a violent form of small-pox, and scarcely a house in that village escaped without paying a death- toll, Of course, when too late, a system of betterdrain- age was vigorously adopted; and the question for Stockton Heathpeople to decide is, whether they would ; like their sanitary arrangements and sewerage schemes thoroughly attended to (and, as T have already stated, only a Corporation could deal effectively with such a. problem) before or after an epidemic ? I am no alarmist ; I am only recording, in cold type, what every reader knows—only the glamour of cheap rates, acts upon many otherwise sensible businest men, such asthe announcement of a " Sale " acts upon a woman. with amania for bargain-hunting, all other considera- tions being merged and lost sight of in that most decep- tive.of all words-T" Cheapness,"

(3) Touching briefly upon the actual incidence (or "fall ") of the cheaper rates—this nettle only needs firmly grasping, and it then tends to help, rather than hinder, incorporation. Let us look at Stockton Heath residential list, and we find that (as stated in my last, Saturday's letter) most of the people—whether employs or employer—depead upon Warrington for a livelihood. Very well—

(a) The employer pays a larger amount, in rates, upon his Warrington premises, because he—and probably some of, his staff—do not contribute to the town's rates, the quota on their residences. That it to say, the natural growth of good-class houses, instead of swelling the assessment of the Borough, is being built, and is going to swell the rates of, a district outside of the Borough. -(1)) The employee, by running away from the town's rates, does, to a certain small extent, injure his employer's interests; because, if the employia lived in Warrington, he •would be contributing towards the rates, which are falling, more and more,- upo n business premises, for lack of sufficient, increase of good residential property within the Borough. T used just this line of argument, this morning, with a keen, hard-headed resident of Stockton Heath, who is employed by an important Warringtonfivm. He frankly avowed his antagonism to my incorporation scheme, and said that he and many others lived at Stockton Heath, purposely to escape the Warrington rates. Fancy poor Warrington providing electric cars, and other improvements, and many of us (myself included) not paying our share of the burden! I pointed out to ray friend, that, as his employer's burden of town's rates increased, in might make a small difference in the power to allow advances of salary—and tbiit even if this. only had an influence of a shilling or so a week, it would more than neutralise any pecuniary benefit my friend could hope to obtain by keeping outside the Borough. From his evident surprise at the argument, I gathered that he had never examined this many-sided rating- question minutely, and his case is probably typical of many other opponents of incorporation. (4) A weighty point for consideration, as bearing upon incorporation, is the price of gas at Stockton Heath. A nett difference of sixpence per thousand, in gas, becomes—virtually—a contribution to the Warring- ton Municipal rates, and yet without carrying with it either the merit of being a voluntary subscription; or the advantage of being a part, of a corporate whole. Let our smart business men please ponder over this short paragraph. I had prepared further notes, but I have already tres- passed unduly upon your space. I shall be glad to hear from those who agree with the idea of incorporation of Stockton Heath with War- rington. What is everybody's business is nobody's business, so for want of a better champion, I have stepped forward, but I will be pleased to stand aside if any well-known public man will take up the subject. I have, _myself, been an observer of local affairs, over 10 years, before venturing to express my opinions ; and always as willing to follow as to lead. There is as much room for, and need of, knighterrantry in the prosaic life of a municipality or a parish, as over.there was in the days of chivalry and doughty deeds. • For instance, what an opportunity exists' if t may respect- fully say so, for Sir Gilbert, bart. Myself an many others regard him not only as a future Member for the Borough (in which I trust Stockton Heath will by then be included), but as something even far greater—he is one of the chief natural leaders of Warrington district, and it has been well said that "every man's opportuni- ties are as his might." in conclusion, I always believe in a definite programme or target to aim at, sot am venturing to suggest an ele- mentary programme for Stockton Heat&, and I should be pleased to have other items sent me by any readers who take an interest in local progress : (1) incorporation with Warrington. - (2) A 5 minutes' car-service. • (3) Later posting of evening letters. (4) Pressure upon the Ship Canal Company to. withdraw.the swing-bridge advertisement hoardings, which disfigure the approaches to Fairfield-road and Ellesmere-road. (5) Uniform price of Stockton Heath gas with Warrington. (6) Thorough overhauling of sewage schemes. (7) High-level bridge at Stockton Heath. (8) Pressure on railway, to dispense with Wilderspool-road, (main-line) level-crossing. (9) An endeavour to get the Ship Canal Company to avoid opening the swing bridge say, between 8.30 and 9 am., and between 1.30 and 2 p.m., to spare business people from delay in reaching War- rington at important periods of the day. Of course, some portions of this programme • must necessarily wait for Stockton Heath's incorporation with Warrington.—Yours faithfully, H. P. HUGHES.
Stockton Heath, 7th April, 1903.

_ - - • • EASTER HOLIDA I'S AT EARLESTOWN. The various works at Earlestown and Newton will cease work on Thursdayevening for the Easter holidays and remain closed until Tuesday morning at nine o'clock. If the weather should be line there is sure to be a large exodus of holiday makers, and especially so from the Nriaduct Works, where there will be a big issue of privilege tickets to all parts of the kingdom. So far no home attractions are arranged, although for Good Friday the Earlestown football club have arranged atixture with Ashton Wanderers.At present the outlook for holiday weather is not very promising but it is hoped the Clerk will be on his best behaviour.

P.S.A. In place of the usual meeting on sittlday last, the Earlestown and District P.S.A. held, 3 musical after- noon. Mr. E. Dickens presided over a fairly large attendance. An excellent programme was submitted. The choir rendeted How beautiful upon the moun- thins " and" The Heavens are telling' " in a very able manner. Mr. Glftve sang " The Toiler " and " Behold T stand at the door "was rendered by Mr. Hamblett. Miss Lucy Stronach sang " The Heavenly Voice "in ' excellent style. A recitation " Little Jim" was de- livered by Mr. S. Kenney. The No. 1 Brass Quartette Prize Party contributed three selections. Miss William- eon accompanied at the piano and Mr.E. Smith presided. at the organ.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SCENE ON A TRAMCAR-DRIVER AND CONDUCTOR ASSAULTED-SMART PENALTY.

A scene occurred on a Warrington Corporation tram car on Saturday evening as a sequel to which Patrick O'Hara, 271, Liverpool-road, appeared before Mr. F', Monks and other magistrates on Aonday. There were three charges against him—namely, assaulting Thomas Alfred Ince, the conductor of the car travelling to Sankey Bridges at 6.30 on Saturday evening, assaulting John Thomas Clarke, the driver, and wilfully breaking a window of the oar, doing damage to the extent of 40s,— He pleaded guilty—Mr. Stanley Wilson, deputy Town Clerk, prosecuted and said defendant wasa passenger on the 6.30 oar from Rylancis-street to Sankey Bridges. When the car reached the "Ship Inn" a witness named Nield entered, and desired to sit be- tween the defendant and a friend of his. There was plenty of room, but defendant refused to allow him to sit there whereupon Nield took a seat on the other side. Defendant appeared to have taken offence at this and commenced to use very bad language. When the car reached Pickmere-street the conductor went inside and warned the defendant who, however, continued to use bad language. After proceeding a short distance, the car was stopped and the conductor requested the defendant to leave. Defendant refused and after' making use of disgusting language struck the conductor se!ierat times and also kicked him about the legs. The driver %vent to the conductor's assistance and defendant struck him several blows. A straggle ensued and defendant in attempting to strike the driver pushed his elbows through one of the windows, causing the damage complained of. Great diffi- culty was experienced in getting the defendant into the street. P.C. Clough came on the scene and defendant continued to be very violent. Eventually P.C. Wools Callr3 to Clough's assistance and defendant quietened down for some time. He was taken part of the way to the Police Station in a car. He made use of filthy language and the officers,Prad great difficulty in getting him to the lock-up. Defendant was under the intlaence of drink but was not drunk. Tais was one of the worst cases experienced since the inauguration,of the tram system in the town.—The magistrates imposed a fine of 40s. and costs with the alternative of a month's imprisonment.
A WO3I..AN'S VIOLENCE AT WARRINGTON.

Annie. Smith, a notorious character, appeare,d in the doe:: at the Warrington Police Court en Moinhy, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Parker-street at. 12.10 on Sunday morning, with assault- ing P.C. Hen itt at theiPolice Station and smashing four panes of glass in the charge ()lice, anda cell window.— Constable Hewitt stated that at ten minutes past twelve on Sunday morning he saw the prisoner in Parker- street. She was shouting excitedly that she had killed a man at Bridge-foot. He told her to go away and she turned round and said she would kill him. He took her to the Police Station. Soate other prisoneri were just being put into the cells, and he took her into the • waiting room. while he turned to speak to Sergeant Williamson she struck him in the face and scratched him near the eye and then picked up a chair and "put it :through four panes of glass."— Sergeant Williamson corroboratei, and said prisoner had not been in the cell an hour before she smashed the window with her shoe. She afterwards asked for a drinkand was given ktin with water in. A little later he heard another noise and found her banging the tin against the wall.—Prisoner was very defiant in the dock arid used filthy language. She said she would like to get six months.—The Chief Constable said prisoneronly came out of gaol on Saturda.yafter serving three months ifor theft. That was her 35th appearance. She was nearly always in gaol or the workhouse.—The Chairman said prisoner would have to go to goal for six months. prisoner: I can do that on my head. (Descending to the calls): Cheer up! We'll soon be dead!

div.head: Minor Cases.
div.p: Minor Cases.
Wavington Borough Police Court.
MONDAY.—Before tr. F. Monks (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, and Messrs. Birchall, Hayward and

Thomtop. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Walter Boswell wa-s summoned for cruelty to two horses by travelling them whilst in an unfit state on March 31st.—P.C. Clough said he was on duty in Wilson Patten-street and saw the defendant in charge of two horses. They were both lame and could scarcely walk.—lnspactor Print gave evidence, .aud said the horses had been destroyed.—A fine of 10s. was imposed. CoNsTABLF: AssA.ULTED.—John Joseph Jackson, of no settled abode, was charged with havin,, been disorderly in Bridge-street on Saturday night and assaulting P.C. Andrews.—The constable said prisonerjwas dancing and shouting and caused a crowd to collect. Witness told hilt to ha quiet but he refused and seized witness by the leg. On being taken into custody he threw himself on the ground and kicked witness on the shins.— Prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
MONDAY.—Before _Si! It. Brooke (in the cha.ir), and

Mr. J. Ockleaton. A TROUBLESOME GIRL.—Mary Ellen Dykes, of Speakman-street, was charged with throwing stones is Devonshire-square.—P.C. Preston stated that on the 30th:of March he saw the girl throwing stones at the pedestrians,and one of the missiles hit a girl over the eye. Mr. Johnson (magistrates' clerk) said that the girl had previously been before the Court for a similar offence and committed. He asked the governor of the prison to report on the girl's conduct and mentalcondition. A reply was received that the girl was an epeleptic and should be carefully watched.—After consultation the girl and her father, James Dykes, were hound over to keep the peace in stuns of £2. MINOR Casms.—For allowing his dog to be at large -without a collar with name attached, William Leigh was fined ss. and costs.—Thetnas Hall was fined the costs 4s. 6d. or in default seven days for allowing the chimney of his dwelling house to be on fire on the 30th March.—P.C. Brayford proved the cases.—Annie Eliza- beth Morgan, Northwieh. was summoned for using obscene language.—Defendant's excuse was that a boy threw astone at her and hurt her.—Defendant was fined Jos. and costs or seven days.
