WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET. The Building Inspector having resigned, the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee have passed a resolution to the effect that the Surveyoradvertise for applications for the office, and that he offer a salary of £lOO per annum, rising by £5 a year to a maximum of £l2o.—At a meeting on the 12th March the committee conferred with the members of the Property Purchasing Commintee with respect to thelaying out of the surplus land ia Bridge-street, when it was resolved that the plan of the surplus land, as amended, be approved; also that the sum of £2.25 be paid to the executor of the late John Pierpoint, deceased, for the purchase of four ireehold cottages numbers 20 and 21, Dial-street, and 1 and 2 Rose-yard. At a meeting on the 18th March, it was agreed that the Town Clerk be authorized to offer the sum of .C 3,300 for the purchase of the premises near Market-gate, occupied by Messrs, Holmes and Booth, which are advertised to be sold by public, auction. At another meeting the committee decided that the Town Clerk address a letter to the Co inty Councils of Lancaster and Chester, on the subject of widening the main roads contiguous to the borough. Councillor BENNETT moved the adoption of the minutes; in the absence, through illness, of Alderman Sutton. He said that according to his recollection the suggestion with respect to the laying out of the surplus land in Bridge-street was not approved. There was some discussion as to the precise form of laying out Market-gate, and it was decided to discuss the matterat a later meeting. He should like to withdraw the minute for the present. Cminciller WiraiNsoN seconded, and the minutes with the exception named, were approved. AN ORDER WHICH WENT WRONG.

At a meeting of the Health Committee a letter was real from the Corporation of Brighton, requesting the Warrington Corporation to make a representation to the Local Government Board as to the necessity of legislation with regard to sewage-contaminated shell- fish, and it was resolved "That, in the opinion of this committee, it is urgently necessary in the interest of the public health that legislation should be enacted by Parliament for the protection of the public against the danger to health arising from the consumption of oysters, and other shellash derived from sewage- polluted sources and that the President of the Local Government Board be respectfully requested to intro- duce such a measure into the nest Session of Parlia- ment." At a meeting held on the Ist April it was resolved "That the following report of the sub-com- mittee b 3 approved 20th March, 1903. After going through the various quotations for the grates, mantels, &c., for the administrative ward of the infectious diseases hospital, the sub-committee recommend the acceptance of the lowest tenders, viz., that of Messrs. Williams and Clayat £78,a130 a "Herald" range at £25, and also asaiall open fireplace from Skeltons, Ltd., at £1 13s. 9d., for the toolhonse.—Signed JOHN WILK IN- SON, JAMES EVANS.' " Alderman S3IE ['HURST moved the confirmation of the minutes, ia the absence of Alderman Sutton, and alluded to the resolution :—"That the tender of the Mersey Electric Lighting Company for the wiring of theNo.l ward at Aikin-street hospital at £l5 be accepted." There had been a little mistake and the tender had been given to Ingram's owing to the fact that the quotation was signed by Mr. Ingrain, who had gone to the Mersey works. Another ward had still to be done, and the tender, which was of a similar amount, would be given to the one who should have had the previous work. The DEPUTY-TOWN CLERK suggested that the resolu- tion should be withdrawn. Alderman SMETHURST agreed, and the minutes were agreed to with that exception. STMET-MAKING—IMPORTANT POINTS FOR

PROPERTY OWNERS. The Paving and sewerage Committee have passed resolutions to the effect that the Finance and Estate Committee be requested to consider the. advisability of extending the period allowed for the payment of street- making expenses; that the portion of Liverpool-road in front of the church of the Sacred Heart be paved the full width with wood blocks ; that the Surveyor be in- structed to report upon the best means of dealing with the sewerage in the Orford district ; and that William Sanderson be appointed foreman ganger at the wages of £2 per week.—The committee considered the advisability of increasing the staff of the Borough Surveyor's de- partment, whereupon it was resolved :—(1) that the salary of Mr. W. G. Longdin be increased to £lOO a year, with an additional increase of ZS per year, to a maximum of £110; (2) that the salary of Mr. 'Sidney Bolton be increased to 15s per week'; (3) that a junior clerk belappointed at a commencing salary of 12s per week, and that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to advertise the appointment in the local newspapers. Councillor TINNION moved the confirmation of the minutes hi the absence of Alderman Heaton, the chair- man of the committee. He said he regretted to have to state that the Aldermen had been seriously ill, but he was pleased to know that he was now somewhat im- proving. (Hear, hear.) As something would no doubt be said later on in reference to the resolution that the Finance and Estate Committee be requested to consider the advisability of extending the period al- lowed for the payment of street making expenses, he ought to say that the committee felt this was entirely. in the hands of the Finance Committee. The resolution was not an expreseion for or against ; itrested with the Finance and Estate committee, and the Paving and Sewerage Committee thought it better to refer it to them.

Councillor Jolts ROBERTS seconded. Councillor Loan alluded to the tender of Messrs. Bennie and Thompson for the labour in forming and paving the new street leading from Lovely-lane to the Infectious Diseases Hospital at 2s. 6d. per superficial yard. He asked if Monks-street was alluded to. COURCHIOT JAMES EVA.NS : YO6, sir. _ _

Councillor Lottr, : Who is going to pay for this? The MAYOR: I am informed the Corporation are. Councillor LORD: I understand there is property on the other side. Are the property owners not going to pay their share? The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK : The property in ques- tion was sold by the Corporation, and one of the con- ditions attached to the sale was that the Corporation should pave and pay for the street. Councillor LORD: Was that condition advertised ? The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK.: Yes, and put in the conditions of sale. Councillor LORD: Thank you. Councillor JAMES Evaxs alluded to the following resolution of the Committtet :—" That the tender of Mr. W. Woodfine, of Ashton-on-Mersey, for the labour required in forming and paving Naylor-street, James- street, Cockhedie-rane, Orford-street, and Arpley-walk, according to plans and specifications, at £199 168. Ild, be accepted." He said he took it that , it was the intention of the Committee to find the material for the construction of new streets in the future. He took advantage of that opportunity of calling the attention of the Council to the fact that this was. rather an important question, at any rate to the property owners of the town. There was a variety of material in the setts that were used in the paving of the streets; there was also a difference in the prices. He found that those interested in the paving of the streets had no evidence as to the price and quality of• the material used on their behalf. He therefore thought it would be wise if the committee when setting out the ' work and advertising for the contract and labour would satisfy those who had to pay the bill later on. There had been considerable agitation of late, and strong re- marks had been made, with regard to the price paid for excavating of streets, and he suggested that the com- inittee should have a survey of the streets taken before they were interfered with, and a surface line prepared showing the depth of the excavation all along the new part of the street, so that persons could see how much they had to pay for. He had spoken privately to the Borough Surveyor about the matter, and he said he thought it would be rather costly to do that. He , thought, however, that the effect would be to settle' what was to-day a burning question in the town. If the committee could do something in the way he had i

suggested it would meet with the general approval of the ratepayers. Councillor TINNION said there was a variety of prices for setts, and the committee had always to keep in mind the value of the houses in the street and the uses to which the street was likely to be put. These matters were always taken into consideration. Pocket, secon- dary or bye-streets -should not of necessity be put to the expense of such adexpensive road as one that was likely to become one of the most important streets. The matter had been before the committee who had en- deavoured as far as they could to allay any suspicion or misunderstanding that seemed to have arisen in one or two cases. At the hut meeting of the committee the Surveyor submitted a sectional plan showing the excava- tions, Ste., and there was no doubt that it.would be a considerable help. It was possible that in the next lot of plans the committee would supply all the information they could. Notice was given that they could be in- spected at the Surveyor's office. Alderman HUTCHINSON seconded, and the motion was carried. THE LAST OF THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

COMPLIMENT TO AtDERMAN SHAW GREEN. The CHAIRMAN, at a meeting of the above committee, on March 19th, intimated that the let April had been fixed all the date the Education Act, 1902, would come into operation and that the present occasion would be the last time the members would meet as a "School Attendance Committee," whereupon it was resolved: "That thiecommittee desire to place on record an ex- pression of their eiacere appreciation of the valuable services rendered to the town during the past 13 years by the Chairman (Mr. Alderman Shaw Green), who has always taken the .warmest interest in the educational welfare of the borough." The final report of the com- mittee, which we published in summary last, week, was also presented and adopted: _ _ _ _

Coimcillor ELLISON -movDd the confirmation of the minutes in the absence of Alderman Shaw Green, and alluded to the final report of the committee. He said they would not meet again as a committee, and he wished, therefore to call attention to the last resolution placing on record the appreciation of the valuable ser- vices rendered to the town by Alderman Shaw Greeu during the past 13 years. He was sure they all deeply regretted the Chairman's absence through illness, but hoped hs would soon be restored to health. (Hear,hea.r). _

Councillor ROGERS seconded. Councillor BENNETT said the Alderman had devoted himself to the work of the committee with the most commendable earnestness and the report which he hoped all had read, was eloquent evidence of the suc- cess which had attended his labours. It had nob been a popular committee, but it had beenahard working com- mittee, and tho members deserved honour. (Applause.) Alderman HUTC.FIENSON greatly approved of the reso- lution with reference to the Alderman who, he said,had been a most exemplary chairman, characterised at all times by his ability, diseretion, and kindness. (Hear, hear.)

Councillor JAM IS EVANS asked if the sum of £3O, the annual donation to the Ship Clio, was included in the estimates? If theco-nmittee paid the fixed charges to the Clio he saw no reason for a special donation. Councillor W. ROBERTS : I don't think that matter arises on to-night's minutes. Alderman fitrromNsos : It does not.

Councillor W. ROBERTS: It has to be a special vote at the proper time,and, therefore, it is not a matter for discussion to-night, T take it. Councillor ELLISON : The £3O is allowed by the county and does not come out of the rates.
Couheillor JAMES EVA-NS: We pay it. The MA.YOrt : lam informed it is included in the estimates.

Councillor JAMES EVANS : Then I was perfectly in order. I raise this matter on principle. The authorities charge us ss. per head, and if that does not pay it is no fault of ours. The INIA.von : Do you wish to have an amendment?
CouacillOr JAMB i EVAN : I think I shall have an opportunity of discus3ing the matter later on with the Education Committee. The minutes were carried. TOWN HALL, PARK AND BATHS.

The minutes of this comMittee, were moved for con- firmation by Alderman Stnethurst, who alluded to Mrs. Crostield's gift. He said they would soon have the new greenhouse up, and he believed with its contents, it would be an ornament to the town. The new private baths were opened, and they were now as well equipped a/any town in Lancashire for swimming s,nd private bat. (Applause.) Counzillor UPSON asked whether anything was con- templated in regard to the recreation ground in Orford- lane. In winter it was nothing but a mud-hole and in summer a dust-heap. (Laughter.) Councillor ELLISON, on behalf of the Open Spaces Sub-Committee, said they contemplated having a meeting shortly and taking the whole question into consideration.

Councillor L'Mtp pointed out that the amount in the estimates did not cover the tender of Mr. T. J. Lee for 1,000 towels, and 500 pairs of bathing drawers. Alderman SMETHURST explained that since the esti- mate was made they found that the extensions necessit- ated a larger contract for these goods.
The miniites were then conflrmea. MAR!CETS COMNarTEE.—THE LAVATORY ATrENDANTS.

1 A meeting of the Markets Co umittee was held on March 30th, when it was resolved that Mr. John Elliot be appointed attendant for the gentlemen's lavatories I at 14s. per week, and Miss Jane Jones attendant for the ladies' lavatories at lls. per week; resolved also that . permission be granted to the committee of the May 'Day horse parade to Me the fair ground off Orford-lane I for the purpose of assembling and judging turnouts on Saturday, the 2nd May. Alderman Hu II:HINSON proposed the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor ROGERS seconded, and called attention to the appointment of the attendants to the new lava- tories. There had been correspondence in the Press charg- ing the Comfiiittee with paying a starvation wage. For the information of the Council he produced a statement of wages paid in various other towns, showing that the reniuneration.,offerecl by Warrington was a fair average.
Councillor W. ROB ER-TS said tile Committee would le prepared to re-consider the matter at the expiration of 3 months.
THE PROFIT ON GAS.-£4,030 IN RELIEF OF
THE RATES.

A meeting of the Gt.; Committee was held on the 6th March. The Borough Trea.aurer atteneled the Com- mittee and was informed by the Chsirman tha.t this Com- mittee would, he considered, be able to provide a sum of £4,000 in relief of the rates for the ensuing year. The confirmation of these minutes MIS moved py the DEPUTY MAYOR, and seconded by Councillor JiofiN ROBERT:3.

Councillor W. RORULT3 Enid he would like to con- gratulate the Chairman of the Gas Committee upon the very pleasing para.graph (quoted above) stating that the Cammittee would be able to provide :£4,000 in relief of the rates. (Hear, hear.) That was one of the best bite of news that they had had for a very long time, and he hoped that next year the Chairman would be able to repeat the (lose. (Laughter.) _ _ _

'Councillor Donis asiod lift balance sheet had been produced showing that this .C 4.000 had Ip?eit realised. The DEPUTY MAYOR said that as yet they had not had time to produce their balance sheet,and this was an estimate.
The minutes were then adopted. THE SHIP CANAL ACTION. CONGRATULATIONS UPON THE RESULT. "WON UPON EVERY POINT."

Alderman BOLTON, in moving the minutes of the Rivers Committee, said he would like to congratulate the Council upon the judgment obtained in she case of the Warrington Corporation versus the Manchester Ship Canal Company, which had been in their favour (Applause.) He was pleased to say that they had won upon every point, and not only was the judgment that they should have an eight-foot draught at all times but also that if one or- even two dredgera could not do it more must be employed until the depth was right. (Applause,) The eight-foot draught would have to be kept up at all times, and the Ship Canal Company would now understand that the Corporation intended to have what they were entitled to. (Heal hear.) They I had secured to Warrington one of the best things they ! had ever had with regard to the river. (Applause). ' Councillor BENNETT, in seconding, said they had every reason to sincerely congratulate themselves upon this decision. What they had gained was what was right and fair and what had been right from the first, but it was nice to have it confirmed by a legal decision. (Applause.) The MAYOR said not only the Town Council but the whole town had every reason to be pleased, and they , could well congratulate themselves upon the result. ' They could also congratulate the Town Clerk upon the manner in which he had carried the matter through. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BOLTON: And the Borough Surveyor, ' and- The MAYOR: Yes. The minutes, which were of a formal character, were then carried. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTER. Alderman SMETHURST proposed the minutes of this committee and read a letter from the postmaster con- gratulating the brigade on its efficient help at the recent I G.P.O. fire. The alderman mentioned also that the , fireman who was injured was home ae*nin but would be unable to attend his duties for sometime. They were glad that his life was saved. (Hear, hear). Councillor DUNCAN seconded, and the minutes were confirmed.
COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON WANTS TO KNOW. THE LOAD ON THE ELECTRICITY PLANT.

Councillor PEMBERTON asked the Chairman of the Electricity Committee :—How many times has the load of our largest engine been exceeded? To what amount? And for what length of time? At what time of the day did it take place? What was the reason ? Alderman MONKS replied to these questions seriatim. There were four occasions, he said, upon which the load had been exceeded, namely, upon Nov. 10th, 11th, 24th and Jan. 26th. Tn the first instance, Nov. 10th, the load was exceeded by 9.18 kilowats ; upon Nov. 11th the load was exceeded by 15 kilowats; upon Nov. 24th by 66.8 kilowats ; and upon Jan. 26th by 20 kilowats.

div.head: IMPORTANT TO ALL.
div.p: IMPORTANT TO ALL.

With regard to the length of time, the excess upon the first occasion was 15 minutes; second occa- sion, 20minutes ; third occasion, one hour anda half,and upon the fourth occasion, 30 minutes. With regard to the time of day, it was somewhere between 4 o'clock and 6 o'clock in the afternoon upon each of the dates named. The question. "What was the reason ?" was rather more difficult because he did not know what it meant. The facts were that the customers of the station asked for current, and they could not prevent them from taking it if they turned their switches. It was only necessary to say that the customers required such an amount, that they overloaded the station. That was the difficulty that the committee had foreseen, and to meet whieh they were bringing before the Council the suggestion that the station should be increased. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND THE

div.head: ELECTRICITY COMMITTEE. THE LETTING OF CONTRACTS. CRITICISM AND ANSWER.
div.p: ELECTRICITY COMMITTEE. THE LETTING OF CONTRACTS. CRITICISM AND ANSWER.

The electricity and Tramways Committee at a meet- ing on the 15th March, considered the report of Messrs Preece and Cardew on the tenders received for the pro- posed extensions, whereupon it was resolved that the following tenders be accepted :—(1) Messrs Babcock and Wilcox for the supply of Boilers and Pipeworic according to specification at £3,282; (2) Messrs Siemens Brothers for the supply of Engines and Dynamos ac- cording to specification, at .£11,434; (3) Messrs Kelvin and White for the supply of Switchboard according to specification, at £416 15s. The acceptance of these minutes was proposed by Alderman Monks. Councillor PEMBERTON moved that the minute relat- ing to the above tenderS be referred back,and commenced a lengthy indictment of the committee and the method of allotting tenders, which he had ready typed. Councillor DODDS seconded for the reason that the expenditure was large and the work did not appear to have been submitted to open competition, and that Messrs Preece and Cardew were to have a commission of 21 per cent., which he did not consider advisable. He hoped also, that out of respect for the trouble Coun- cillor Pemberton had taken he would be allowed as much latitude as possible.

Councillor Rosiwrs : I think Councillor Pemberton has had a very patient hearing to-night, and I am bound to admit he has given some of us information we did not possess before. He could not, however, see the wisdom of referring the minutes back, as he took it that Messrs. Preece and Cardew had been their profes- sional advisers. He supposed also that the committee Atts practically unanimous, and if that was so they should give the committee credit for having gone into the matter fully, carefully, and with every desire to keep down expenses._ .

Councillor lAMES EVAAS said there wore one or two poiribs which might not have been considered before. If he understood right the committee invited tenders and specified whose engines they should be. That was not open competition. Another point was that they were not needing two ;Anginas. Whatever there might be in economising on quantities he hardly thought there were any possibilities of economising on quantities such as thee and material such as this. If this particular kind of engine must be tendered for then he was at variance with the CoMmittee on the question of com- mission. It was paying Messrs. Preece and Cardew commission for advisington something their own engineer had had practical experience of. Alderman iVlosiKs in reply said the first reason he would urge why these matters should not be referred back was because there was a certain amount of urgency The figures he had given showed that last winter the electric station was considerably over-loaded. There were other figures far more important. The cap tcity of the station was altogether 1.1,0J0 kilowit, consisting of four engines. They might leave, for light and power Nos. two and three out of ;tie Ttes-,ion, because they were both required for tramway work. The tramways did not at present take up the full lead of both these but they must have two engines in order to provide against break-down. What they proposed was to make necessary provision for lighting and .driving onli. For that they had Nos. 1 and 4. They had new customers every week and there was every reason to believe that the total number of new customers between now and next summer would increase in the same propor- tion as in each previous year. Unless something was done they would risk a very serious breakdown. The 500 kilowat engine had been overloaded and assuming they-could take one of the tramway engines—which had been done—they had only 350 kilowatts to take the load of the larger engine. If anything had happened to the;soo kilowat engine and they had had to rely upon the combined 350 kilow its of the two spare engines. every day last winter from October to February, the actual load at the station would have been considerably in excess of the capacity of these two engines. For three and a half months they would have been unable to supply the customers in the town with the current they wanted—and there was a serious penalty for fail- ing to supply. They wanted the new set of engines in order to cope with the increased load they were bound to have next winter. The second set would also be necessary in twelve mouths time if not in less time. The committee were Unanimous in this matter, withthe exception of Councillor Pemberton, who showed his want of unanimity bY staying away from the meetings of the committee.

Councillor PEMBERTON : I have only been away when I have been ill. Alderman MONKS: Ido not know what the reasons are but I have noticed your absence. Pro. ceading, if Councillor Pemberton had been present he would have heard all he had said that night discussed in committee. His statement that they had 600 kilowats in reserve was not correct. The only actual reserve they had was one 100" kilowat set when the load was beyond the capacity of the 500 kilo. set. With 'reward to the limitation of the tenders. They were not restricting competition. The tenders recommend ed for acceptance that night were at a proportionately less cost for the size of the engine than any they had put down before, and at a less cost than any that had been supplied recently to other Corporations by the same makers. That was one of the advantages they got from employing consniting engineers. Every week they were considering tenders suclaas these. Notwithstand- ing that the advertisements specified one kind of engine they had tenders for other engines, some cheaper. Out of 17 tenders altogether they selected the sixth from the lowest,pecause they knew from experience that the engine in question cost less to maintainand was cheaper in the long run. The first cost was not the most im- portant thing in buyinean engine.(Hear.hear.) There was '' a good deal also in gating their engines uniform, so Ithat the engineers could be familiar with them. Practi- cal engineers would assure them there was something in it. (Hear, hear.) The Committee had carefully thought these matters out during the past six or eight months. If Mr. Pemberton did not choose to Usk any competent member of the Committee, or the engineer, for hi q in- formation he muit go without. They would have bees pleased to give it him. Hecould assure the Council that every care had been taken in recommending these tenders. (Applause) Alderman BOLTON said he Was present at the meeting' of the committee when the tenders were accepted. Other tenders did not comply with the specifications. He supported Alderman Monks and emphasized the necessity for having a reserve of power. A vote was then taken on the amendment, only Coun- cillors Pemberton, Dodds, Lord, and James Evans vot- ing for it. The minutes were then comfirmed. THE PROPOSED INQUIRY. COUNCILLOR TINNTON'S RESOLUTION RESCINDED. THE MAYOR AND THE NON-TRADERS.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee on March 30th, it was resolved: "That the resolution of the Council on page 105 of the printed proceedings, and having reference to a proposed examination of the ac- counts of the Corporation,and to an inquiry into alleged illegal trading of members of the Council with the Cor- poration, be rescinded, and that in pursuance of the re- solution of the Council of the 3rd March last, Alderman Bolton and Councillors James Evans and Tinnion be appointed to confer with three representatives of the Non-Municipal Trading Committee." Councillor DODDS pointed out that the resolutioi which it was proposed to rescind referred to all trading with the Corporation by members of, the Council and not to alleged trading, Only. After the confer- ence had been held he did not want the Council to say they were only going to inquire into the alleged illegal trading. .
The-TowNCLER,K. mid the intention wits to rescind the whole of Clunciller Tinnion's resolution.

Councillor TENNION slid he had not the slightest ob- jection to the recinding of what had been called the " Tinnion " resolution, of which he was not ashamed, if it was the only reason that would stand in the way of an inquiry and understanding between the Corporation and the Non-trading Collimate°. He wanted them to get at closer quarters, and he was willing to withdraw in favour of a resolution that would be mutually accept- able and get rid of the agitation not onlyto the satis- faction of the members of the Council and the Non- Traders but of the whole of the ratepayers of Warring- ton. Councillor Dodds was quite right in pointing out that his (the speaker's) resolution provided for an in- quiry into all trading. Councillor DODDS then said that the Mayor, in a letter to the "Times," referred to the Non-trading party as a small but demonstrative Section of the people. (Hear, hear.) That had given very great offence to a large majority of the townspeople, and he wanted to knew whether the Mayor was prepared to withdraw that statement, (cries of " Order and "Rubbish "), or whether he (Councillor Dodds I was to tell his constituents that it was untrue and ought to be withdrawn.

Councillor W. RougnTs : I hope the Mayor won't answer such an insolent question. (Laughter.) The MA von: As far as the question is concerned I am advised it does not come before the Council. I may have given a personal opinion, but I don't see that need go further. If I was wrong I was. wrong. Councillor W. ROBERTS: You are quite right, sir— (laughter)—and everybody thinks so too. _
The minutes were Confli:med. FINANCE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee held on the 9th March, the Borough Treasurer presented the follow- ing report as the result of his interview with the Local Government Board regarding the financial adjustment between the countyand the borough :—"The Board have

agreed to certify the discontinued grants under Section 22 as £3,063, and our share of the new grant under Section 26 as £1,619 less £132 contained in both grants, making a total of 44,550, the county having agreed to these figures. The Loeal Government Board will now proceed to issue the Order accordingly." The minutes were approved. The discussion on the Borough Budget is reported in another column.
MUNICIPAL BOWLING GREENS.
COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON SUGGESTS THREE.

Connelllor PEMBERTON moved the following motion, of which he had given notice: "That this Council forthwith provide three public bowling greens; one in Queen's Gardens' one in the Park adjoining the Town Hall, and one in Victoria Park,Latchford." ICouncillor WILLIAM ROBERTS: Haa.not a resolution been adopted by the Council on this question? 1 The MAYOR: The question has been discussed. 1 Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS: A resolution was before the Council a short time ago and you, Mr. Mayor suggested at the close of the discussion that the Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee should submit a scheme for the provision of one bowling green. The MAYOR: I think it was only a tentative resolu- tion. We have had no report on that decision. I Councillor PEMBERTON: I don't think you will have any report. Continuing he said there was very little done by the Council for the working-classes. Many Ipromises were made at election times but they were forgotten afterwards. His proposal for establishing bowling greens was for the benefit of poor people. It was not a new proposal for there were municipal bowl- ing greens in many towns and he was pleased to hear 1 that some of them were paying. In a neighbouring town there were three bowling greens under the control of the Council and the return from these greens averaged £5O each, and the authorities considered they were earning a profit. Exceptions had been taken to the provision of a muni- cipal bowling green on the ground that grass would not grow in Warrington. But if grass would grow on the lawns of the Conservative and Liberal Clubs he did not see why it would not grow in the public parks. This was a workingman's question—a question of finding some proper recreation—and carrying into practice what a great many people desired. , The MAYOR: This matter of providing bowling greens is still under the consideration of the Town Hall. Parks and Baths Committee and they have actually gone so far as to ask for estimates. These estimates will come before the Council in due course. Councillor PEMBERTON : It ought to be done forth- with. The committee has been so long in thinking about it. Councillor UPSON seconded the resolution and sug- gested that a bowling green should also be provided in Orford Ward.
Councillor BENETT thought the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee had shown an indisposition to meet the wishes of the public in the matter.

Councillor JOHN ROBERTS said he wished Councillor Pemberton could have seen his way to be satisfied with one bowling green as a trial. (Hear, hear.) He did not think they could work a bowling green during the season for less than about tl per week, and the cost of laying a green would be something like £3OO. The cost of the three greens would probably be about £BOO. If Coun- cillor Pembeiton wanted to save the ratepayers' money he (Councillor Roberts) could not see why he should press this matter. Councillor W. ROBERTS said he thought that after the repeated discussions in the Council and the favourable reception the subject had always received the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee ought not to lose a single moment in providing at least one bowl- ing green. He thought. the provision of one green as an experiment would be very satisfactory all round. He was very dubious about municipal bowling greens being paying concerns. His experience of bowling greens had been that the bowling green proper had been , a source of considerable loss but a profit had been made by the sale of intoxicating drinks. If the Council could get a licence for each green they could no doubt make them a very handsome source of profit but probably , that would be objected to by the licensed victuallers. He suggested that the Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee should take it as a direct instruction to provide one bowling green forthwith. Councillor JAMES EvA.Ns said he took it that the greens would be provided as counter-attractions to the institutions to which bowling greens were at present attached. On social and moral grounds the Corporation were obliged, if they were considering the highest interests of the people to make some provision for the requirements of those who sought the recreation of bowling He was in favour of one green being provided in a central position and hoped the committee would soon proceed with the work.

Alderman BOL-T-0;1-s-afillivas nearly ten years since a municipal bowling green was first suggested. Unsucces- ful experiments were made in the recreation ground in the Park. At the ton end of the ground observations were taken in regard to the amount of smoke which was blown in that direction. It was found that the rain could not fall on that piece of land without washing so much smoke that the green would not be satisfactory unless a green house were erected over it. (Laughter.) Some bowling greens in Warrington had to be renewed every two or three years. The com- mittee did not think they ought to spene. the ratepfvers' money upon something that they were not certain about. However,if the Council did levy another penny rate the Committee would experiment with the money with pleasure and lay bowling greens in Bank Park, Victoria Park or Queen's Gardens. He thought the members of the Committee were perfectly willing to provide a bowling green if they could be thoroughly satisfied that it would be a success. Councillor CRAIK said that after the very lame state- ment of Alderman Bolton he should strongly support Councillor Pemberton's proposition. In Manchester there were six or seven municipal bowling greens, and they were all paying concerns. in addition to paying their way there was a balance to be handed over to the Borough Treasurer. If they could grow grass in Man- chester for municipal greens, surely to goodness we could grow it in Warrington. He never heard a lamer statement in his life than that of Alderman Bolton as to not being able to grow grass in Warrington. He sugges- ted that there should be two greens. The MAYOR: Would it not be desirable to give instructions to the committee to provide one? . Councillor CRAIK : I am afraid they are past instructing. Councillor TINNION said it seemed to him that Coun- cillor Pemberton was appa.rentlyaskino• for his proposi- tion to be rejected or he would aye made a more reasonable suggestion. The speaker expressed himself in favour of one or two greens but not of one in Queen's Gardens.

Alderman SMETIIURST expressed surprise that such a motion was brought forward by Councillor Pemberton. Continuing he said that no onelhad been more desirous of providing a bowling green than the Chairman of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee,and many of the members. Taking all circumstances into consideration they thought they could not possiLly get a good green. He had a list of seventeen towns where there were municipal bowling greens, and he did not believe that there was one that paid. The workingmen of Warrington were not badly off for bowling greens. He had a list of twenty-four greens in the town; or within a mile of it, and if they were not sufficient for rhe workingmen he did not know what they wanted, There were bowling greens attached to the political clubs, and there was also a green at Arpley. Alderman MONKS said that a strong reason why the resolution should not be passed was because it com- mitted the Council to an expenditure, but they had no idea of what that expenditure would be. He suggested that Councillor Pemberton should withdraw his resolu- tion and submit another one instructing the Borough Surveyor to draw up a specification and get tenders for carrying out the necessary work for one green. The Alderman pointed out that expenditure on bowling greens was not provided for in the estimates which had been submitted. Councillor Loan asked if there were any bowling greens open to the working classes and unattached to the public-houses, political clubs, or private subscrip- tion clubs.

The question was not answered. Councillor PEmsErcros said he thought Councillor Tinnion was the only person in Warrington who would think for a moment that he wanted to have a bowling green in that part of Queen's Gardens which had already been laid out. He was willing to alter his resolution to the effect that oue bowling green be forthwith pro- vided in Queen's Gardens. He did not think any further expense ought to be incurred in connection with that .land until a green had been provided.. The MAYOR said the only course open to 'Councillor Pemberton was to withdraw the resolution and bring forward another at the next Council meeting. Councillor PENIBERTON refuted the suggestion of Councillor Tinnion that he had brought forward the resolution with the intention of having it rejected. He was most earnest in his wish that the scheme should be carried out. It seemed to be the system with the majority of public representatives to talk at election times of what they would do for the workingman but never carry it out in practice. Eventually the motion was withdrawn on the under- standing that the course suggested by Alderman Monks was adopted.
THE PAYMENT OF PRIVATE STREET • ACCOUNTS. PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TIME. MOTION DEFEATED.

Councillor PEMBERTON moved that property owners be allowed ten years in which to pay the cost of the making of private streets. In the course of his remarks he contended that street making came upon many people as a very great hardship. His resolution did not suggest any extra cost to the ratepayers, and therefore he considered it ought to receive no opposition. What did it matter to the Council whether property owners were allowed three years or ten years in which to pay the accounts so long as the extension of time would cost the ratepayers nothing? He knew of cases in which small property owners had had to sell property when street snaking had had to be paid for. Councillor PORSHAW said that if Councillor Pember- ton would make the time seven or eight years he would have pleasure in seconding the resolution. Thu MAYOR said the resolution could not be altered now. _ _
. Councillor FORSHAW seconded the proposition as it stood. He certainly thought property owners were at

the present time very much hampered, and they ought to have a reasonable space of time in which to pay for this expensive street making. Councillor JAMES EVANS was in favour of time being extended, but did not know whether it would be desir- able to make such a great extension as was proposed. At. his request,

. , Alderman FAIRCLOUGH read the following report on •the subject :—Street-making accounts. Balance owing as at 31st March, 1903; interest, £249 ss. 5d.; principal; £9,4,32 16s. id.; total, £9,682 is. 6d. There are 125 accounts at present open, and in 104 cases agreements liave beensigued. There are 28 accounts varying from six months to 2L- years overdue, amounting to about £2,800. Of this amount £2,250 is owing by eight persons as follows: one owes £1095 Bs. 5d., one owes £ll6 6s. 4d.. one' owes £142. Bs. 11d., one owes £lOB 6s. 2d. one owes £ll7 15 10d., . one owes, £293 2s. 11d. one owes £l5l 4s. 11d., and one owes £l4O 18s. ld making a total of £2,255 6s. 7d. About t.:246 10s. has been paid by the above persons in the last six months. During the last six months, since the definite action of the committee £3,220 Is. Bcl. has been received. In answer to Councillor Forshaw, Alderman FAlR- cLoudii said the resolution if passed would not apply to the debtors he had mentioned.

Councillor BURTON said he was rather surprised to hear Councillor Evans say he could not go all the way with the proposition. It seemed to him (Councillor Burton) that Councillor Evans would go a long way to help working men but when it came to helping the in- dustrious workingmen of the town then his hand did not go very far to help them. He believed that if the Corporation could see its way to extend the time for the repayment of the cost of private street making it would save a good deal of trouble and expense. Councillor JAMES EVANS, in making an explanation, said he took it this was not exactly a workingman's question. From the list which had been read out it would be seen that the persons owing money were not all workingmen. It was a question for property owners.

Councillor WHAussox said this was not a working- man's question and he was sorry to see that Councillor Burton had not got a thorough grip of the question. Councillor BURTON: Shall I give some names of workingmen who own property? (" No.") Councillor WILKINSON said the people who refused to pay their street bills were not generally workingmen. The workingmen paid their accounts, but many who were not workingmen, refused to pay. That was why he should opposeany alteration of the time allowed for payment until those who owed street accounts paid them.

• Aldermam MONKS said he believed he was correct in saying that the Local Government Board would not allow the Corporation to lend money to propertyowners on private street accounts for a term of ten years. The present resolution was a sequel to what took place a short time ago when an attempt was made to control the Finance Committee and prevent the committee from taking action for the recovery of the money. It arose from two or three individuals who could well afford to pay and who had persistently refused to pay. These people had tried to defy the Finance Committee and to resist paying the aocounts. Now that they saw that the Council was behind the Finance Committee theyhad commenced to pay their accounts and no doubt would continue to do so.

Councillor CRAIK hoped the Council would support the Finance Committee. The grievance complained of was an entirely imaginary one. The Finance Com- mittee had had the mltter before them on three sep- arate occisions and they could not see their way to change the attitude they had taken. It was not a case of workingmen being unable to pay the accounts but of two or three property owners fighting the committee. Councillor TrxmoN did not think it would be wise to make such a considerable alteration as suggested, from three to ten years. He did not know anyone else who could borrow money at four per cent with practically no security. If the time was extended for the payment of private street accounts he was inclined to suggest that there should be a graduated scale of interest rising from four per cent for the first three years, to five per cent for the next three years and 5i per cent for the remainder.
The MA.YoR : I am told that it is fixed by Parlia- ment at (our per cent.

Councillor frINNION : Then in that case I think we ought to have a detailed statement respecting these, street accounts before we commit ourselves to an ex- tension of time for payment. Councillor PEMBERTON said he did nothold a brief for any man who did not pay his street account. He had in his mind many people who had paid their private street accounts and he marvelled how some of them had been able to pay them out of their limited incomes. He was plepared to say that the Local Government Board did grant a period of ten years within which these accounts could be paid. In a district within 11 miles from that Council Chamber, nwners of property were allowed ten years to pay private street accounts. He understood that the Corporation could borrow money at a little over three per cent, and although there would not be any great profit, there would not be any loss. lie wished to emphatically impress upon them the fact that it was not a question of giving the property owners anything. He knew many people to whom this exten- sion of time to ten years for the payment of private street accounts would have been a great help indeed. On a vote being, taken 8 voted for Councillor Pem- berton's motion and 11 against. The motion was there- fore lost.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Prince of Wales, after spending the Easter recess at Sandringham with his family, will go to Scotland for some salmon fishing. Golf links have been laid down at Balmoral, but hitherto none of the Royal Family have taken very enthusiastically to the game. The Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Fife are both much more fond of fishing, and Princess Victoria pre- fers her bicycle to the golf clubs. It was thought,when the Royal residences were provided with golf links that the King might take seriously to the game, but his Majesty was thinking more of others, and Mr. Balfour, and probably other ministers will appreciate this thoughtfulness, when theyare in attendance at Balmoral. Not many women have any opportunity of practising fencing, but for those who have, no doubt it is an ex- cellent form of exercise. Miss Lowther, who has at- tained such distinction as a swordswoman, writes upon this subject in one of the Reviews, but she does not think that women, apart from a few exceptions, can at- tain to any great skill in fencing. In quick and delicate movements of the wrist, or arm, they are perhaps more than equal to the men but they lack muscular strength, and also the instinct Of fighting, which seems essential in sword play. Still, from many points of view, fenc- ing is a capital exercise, and it is one of which the children of the Duke and Duchess of Fife are very fond. They are now growing tall girls, Lady Alexandra, the elder, will be twelve next month, and Laiy Maud, the younger, is just ten. Womens clubs continue not only to multiply but to increase in their grandeur and ambition. The Ladies' Empire Club, which was started a year or so ago,to pro- vide a common meeting place for the women of this country and the Colonies, soon had to move into more commodious premises. Then followed the Ladies' Army and Navy, the Ladies' Automobile and the latest is the Ladies' Field, where the sporting sentiment will be the principal feature. There will, of course, be a billiard room which is a common adjunct, to most of the women's social clubs, but there will also be a fenc- ing room, and a dog room. The latter is a compara- tively new feature, in clubdom, and the members of the Ladies' Field will run a coach of their own during the summer months.

The King is an enthusiastic motorist, and it is there- fore quite probable that their Majesties may be present at the Gordon Bennett Cup race which will be the principal feature of the automobile fortnight in Ireland next July. The course is a somewhat triangular one extending over 370 miles of roadway, chiefly in Queen's County and Kildare. Roughly speaking,Carlow and Maryborough are the extreme points in the south with Kildare and Kilcullen in the north, where the course is not more than 25 or 30 miles from Dublin. Something like £l,OOO is being subscribed and spent upon improving the condition of the roads, 220 of which are quite straight. It is to be hoped that the affair will be' free from serious accidents which have unfortunately greatly increased in number since the advent of the motor car.

The title—Earl of Dublin—is always held, like that of the Dukedom of Cornwall, by the eldest son of the Sovereign, and therefore the impression that the King holds the title of Earl of Dublin is not correct. It be longs to the Prince of Wales. The King was, of course horn with several Scotch and English titles, but the Earldom of Dublin, was only created by our late Queen in 1850, the year after the King's first visit to Ireland. Each of the sons of the late Queen also had an Irish title conferred upon them. The re-appearance of large sun-spots has already given rise to dismal predictions of a wet summer. Astronomers say that a minimum rainfall is coincident with a minimum of sun-spots, and both conditions have prevailed for several years past. Now that the period of sun-spat frequency is recurring we are told to expect, wet summers, and in that case there will be little de- mand for muslin or other light and airy frocks. Last year the weather was so cold that they could be very little worn, but in spite of these ominous signs we need not yet despair of being able to disport our summer finery before very long. The command that bonnets "—which being inter- preted means bonnets and toques—are to be worn at. the forthcoming Drawing Room at Holyrood Palace, need scarcely have struck the terror into feminine hearts, North of the Tweed, it appears to have done. Toques this spring are dainty and fascinating to a degree and the most delightful bonnets are being shewn and worn. The latest, a poke shape, in drawn chiffon or tulle, which curves away above the ears, and again a little at the back, to admit of the low coiffure, has for its trimming a long curving ostrich plume a little knot of roses tucked in a little to the left in front,and fluffy tulle strings, which wind round the neck, and form a wide spreading bow on the left side. A glance at such bewitching headgear will surely reconcile all women attending the Drawing Room to the term "bonnet." For golf, a recreation many of us womenkind will indulge in this Easter time, nothing is so warm, dries so quickly, or gives such freedom for a full swing, as the knitted woollen blouse. In white such a garment is usually very becoming, but dark red is more economical, and at this season of the year when the weather is, to say the least, uncertain, it looks comfortable. Por bicycling costumes, grey is the favourite color. This is an)excellent choice, as it shows neither dirt nor dust. And with these short cycling skirts, tailors-are building long underskirts—of lining—with one flounce. These women who are contemplating tours, will be eager to patronise the idea, as it will, in many instances,do away with all necessity for a second skirt, moreover it will enable one to wear one's cycling costume upon many other occasions than are possible, when only the one short skirt is supplied. In cycling hats, the newest are in rustic straw' dark biscuit or champagne in tint the shape being akind of idealised sailor,the ',trimmings being of black velvet, secured by small silver buckles Curtains and porti4res of house flannel, is one of the latest notions, and a very economical one too. Of course such hangings must be embroidered, but the de- signs are in every instance bold, and can be very quickly finished off. Tke colours used in the embroidery should repeat those prevailing in the room when the effect will be found to be particularly good. The reader who takes up Mr. Bernard Capes "A Castle in Spain" (Smith Elder and Co. Be.) is not likely to leave the book unfinished. It is unquestionably one of the most thrilling romances, Mr. Bernard Capes has yet given us, and to those ifamiliar with his • Joan Brotherhood," "The Lake ef Wine," and "The Adven- tures of the Comte de Is Muette "this means a great deal. The narrative is brisk and vivid, and the style distinguished.
MADGE

div.head: WARRINGTZN ENTERTAINING SOZIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTZN ENTERTAINING SOZIETY.
First Annual Supptr.

The above sOciety held their first annual supper on Thursday last week at the Saracens Head, Wilderspool, and needless to say the function proved a great success. There were present the Chairman (Mr. R. Whitfield), supported by Messrs. F. Fieldhouse, G. F. Freeman (secretary), E. A Sanders, W. H. Ireland. J. W. Bullen and others. After supper an excellent musical programme was submitted. At the outset the Chairman delivered a short address in which he referred to the progress of the society during the past season. The members had taken part in-no fewer than eleven concerts, exclusive of other concerts at which only a few of the members had been engaged. One pleasing feature of the Society's concerts had been the steady individual improvement of the members— shown at concert after concert—which augured well for the next season. The various gentlemen who had en- gaged them during the season (and here let him give them gm very best thanks of the Society) had invari- ably expressed themselves in the highest terms of the performances, and in most cases had promised them further engagements in the future. The Chairman pro- ceedel to refer to the constitution of the Society and eulogised the services of the musical directors (Messrs. W. IL Kendrick and Fred Fieldhouse), the secretary (Mr. G. F. Freeman), the treasurer (Mr. W. Whittaker), the remaining trembers of the committee (Messrs. E. A. Sanders and G. B. Kendrick), the individual artistes and the orchestra. They ought to •be proud of their combination and he did not think they had any cause to fear in any way the future. Although grateful to all those who had been instrumental in engaging them and procuring engagements for them, next season they would not be content to sit down and wait for engage- ments to come to them, but would engage halls and give concerts at their own risk among those people to whom they were now known, as well as being at hand to fulfil any engagements they might receive. In conclusionhe thanked on behalf of the committee all those who had . contributed to make the Society's operations during tho past season such a success. (Applause.) The SECRETARY (Mr. G. F. Freeman), said the society : had gradually grown into a good sound company, after : several hard struggles, but now he was pleased, as they were, to see them in a flourishing condition.• • The otchestra gave a grand march, and items wsre I contributed by Messrs. F. Fieldhouse, W. H. Ireland, Arthur Griffiths, F. Warburton, J. Ernson (humorist), E. S. Sanders (reciter), and W. Whittaker (whistler). I Mr. Sanders proposed the toast of "The Visitors "to which Mr. J. W. Bullen responded. Messrs. W. H. Kendrick and Frank Booth accompanied and the orchestra gave several selections. The singing of the National Anthem concluded a highly enjoyablaevening. ,

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

The results ot the deliberations of Madame la Mode are now displayed on all sides, and are as charming as they are numerous, which is saying a good deal. In fact, a real dangex is found in this very profusion., for every woman is impulsive, and therefore apt to fall, an easy victim to the fascinations of the all too lovely garments on view, and so exceed her dress allowance. Most of the leading firms are e displaying their early summer models of costumes and coats, blouses and bijouterie, hats and toques, and the variety is truly amazing. There are cheap and yet wonderfully smart coats and skirts for those who are not well off, and elaborate and costly

toilettes for the fortunate few to whom money is of no consideration; while the headgear is suited to all persons and tastes. A survey of the latest styles has served to confirm my previously conceived notion that the latest modes are merely an exaggeration of those of the past six months. Coats are short and of the sac order, made with inserted knife or box-pleats, and trimmed with cord and tassels and lace, while skirts are not so long or trailing as before, but are more elaborate, showing drawings, gatherings, and gaugings in plenti- ttide.l
A pretty hat is given in my illustration trimmed with mauve and pink convolvulus, with the natural-looking leaves and inter- twining stems tied at the back with narrow green ribbon: _ _

When ostrich feathers are employed as a trimming the sterns of the feathers are laid flat on the crown with the feathers them- selves curling softly over the edge of the brim at the back on to the hair of the wearer. Ostrich feathers are not curled so closely as

SMART TOILETTE. they used to be, and are left to their natural fluffy appearance. I have heard it rumoured that the tiny little bonnet which some twenty or so years ago was worn by every debutante, is likely to reappear and become both popular and fashionable J This style of headgear, when not ridiculously small, proved exceedingly becoming to the sweet face of a young English girl, much more so than the so-called bonnet of later years, which was really a glorified hat with strings. I fancy, however, it will be some time yet before the Princess bonnet (as it was formerly called) becomes generally worn, and that meantime the fol- lowers of les anodes will content themselves with the flat-crowned, picturesque hats in 6 vogue:

The smart toilette depicted is made of one of the new open-meshed canvases which, in contradiction to their somewhat fragile appearance, are extraordinarily strong, and stand any amount of wear. The colour employed in this instance is a soft green, made over a lining of dull blue silk, the glint of he silk lining giving a truly charming shot effett The coat is of the sac order, and shows a glimpse of the folded emerald green velvet waistband. A high-shaped band is necessary with this style of loose coat, which practically stops short in the middle of the back, otherwige the waist would not have the trim, neat look necessary to a smart tout ensemble. Some of these loose coats, which are quite the thing of the moment, are as much a cape as a coat, as they are sometimes fashioned more like the looser style of gar- ment. A smart model coatee was made with a series of capes, the back falling loose, while a deep collar of guipure lace gave a dressy finish. The sleeves were of mousseline, matching in tone the pale string colour of the smooth cloth of which the coatee waq made. There are some of the sac coats which attain to three-quarter length, and- consist of a series of overlapping wide pieces of cloth.
AN EVENING GOWN

The fussier and more peculiar these garments are the more chic they seem to be considered. Tussare is sometimes employ-ea for visites and sacs, and these look very modish when trimmed with string-coloured lace of a coarse make, and lined with white silk or soft satin. The most expensive models are lined with mousseline de soie, but this fabric is too delicate to stand much wear.

_ The plain but modish evening gown shown in the third illutration is of sequined net over satin, and would be suitable for almost any occasion. The sequins are silver, and a cluster of crimson roses finish the decolletage. There are some very charming tissues for evening wear, with silver threads interwoven, These look very well as a trimming, oj ferm exquisite toilettes. On nearly all the prettiest gowns lace is introduced, as there is nothing so becoming, for it softens hard lines and can be skilfully arranged to conceal many de- ficiences of form and figure. Empire or Directoire gowns are made of soft clinging satin, with the hem embroidered, and a scarf of soft mousseline or chiffon passed round the figure below the arms, tied in a knot at one side, while the ends are allowed to fall down nearly to the edge of the skirt, where they are finished either by lace or fringe or a frill. With evening dress the hair is generally dressed low, but when drawn up to the crown of the head a fold of tulle is sometimes inter- twined and tied in a bow in front. -
CoQuErTs.

div.head: IMPROVEMENT RATE.
div.p: IMPROVEMENT RATE.

Alderman FAIRCLOUGH moved that the Council make an improvement rate for the year commencing Ist April, 1903, at 3s. in the .£, to be collected by half. yearly instalments. • Alderman MONKS seconded and the motion was agreed to.

div.head: GENERAL SEWERS RATES.
div.p: GENERAL SEWERS RATES.

Alderman FAIRCLOUGH moved that the Council make a general sewers rate for the yearcommencing Ist April, 1903, at 4d. in the 2,.t0 be collected by two half-yearly instalments. Alderman BOLTON contended that '2d. in the £ would be sufficient.
The BOROUGH TREASURER pointed out that a penny rate on the sewers or improvement rates was a very different matter from a penny on the Borough rates. A

div.head: FINAL REPORT OF THE
div.p: FINAL REPORT OF THE
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
26 Years' Work.

tn, con'sequence of the passing of the Education Act 1902, the School AtteadanceCommittee as an executive, committee of the Council ceased to exist on " the appointed day." which was the Ist of April. Its duties, which werenonunenced 23 years ago, will, in future, be performed by the Education Committee or by a sub- committee appointed by that body. Tae Committee have deferred presenting their report for the year ending October last, in order that the figur6s.and information may be extended and brought down, as near as possible to the date on which the duties of the Committee will cease. It has now been issued, and signed by the Chairman. The report states :—As showing.' the increase in the work of this Department since its formation in 1877, a cursory examination of the following figures will be instructive : No. of children Average Year. on the books. attendance Population. 1877 ....... 5,572 .1903 ....... 13,902 _ _12,288 _ 66,000.

Although pressure was brought upon the Council by the Board of Education and the preliminary step taken for the formation of a School Board, and which your Committee felt had become a necessity in the town owing to the great want of school accommodation, it is very satisfactory to knost- that the turmoil and expense of the election and formation of a School Board have been avoided, and the difficulty of dealing with the clerk and officers, which a school Board would have re- quired, has been obviated. Your Committee would em- phasine the necessity which has been pointed. oat in previous reports of additional school accommodation being forthwith provided in several parts of the Borough. INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

! The report of the Chief Inspector states that "There have been twelve ordinary and 27 rota meetings of your ; Cemmittee,to which 1,408 parents or guardians have been summoned. This is an increase of 62, compared with•last year. Your Committee dealt with an average ef 36 cases at each in,?ting. The prosecutions before the magistrates have been 290, being a decrease of 36 ; compared with the previous year. Two examinations 1 for labour certificates have been held during the year; • 56 children were examined, of whom 25 passed, the per- • nentaga of passes being 45, This is still a further de- crease in the number of candidates as compared with the previous year, accounted for I think bya disposition on the part of parents to allow their children to stay at school until 13 years of age. There have been 630 certi- ficates of previous due attendance issued during the year, an increase of about 100 compared with the pre- vious year.

div.head: ACCOMMODATION.
div.p: ACCOMMODATION.

The number of children for whom accommodation is provided in the elementary schools of the borough is 13,596 being exactly the same aslast year. Your com- mittee willnote•that at the present time the schools are not provided to suit the convenience of the children. Note the schools provided in Howley Ward and the scarcity of schools in the Fairfield, St. John's, Orford and Bewsey Wards, whilst the same remarks apply to the Town Hall and St. Austin's Wards on the one hand and the Bewsey, Whitecross, and Latchford Wards on the other. There is great difficulty at the present time in getting children admitted in school especially the back- ward children ; the general cry from the schools is that they are overcrowded, and it is a fact that'they must be admitted, and at the preient rani(' increase of children on the books, in a very short time, there will not be a single vacancy in any school in the borough.

div.head: ATTKSD A.SC E.
div.p: ATTKSD A.SC E.

The average attendance for the year is 11,627 being an increase of 712 over the previous year. The number on the books for the same period is 13,363, an increase of 407, giving a percentage of 87; this is 21 higher than last yekr. There are, however, 1,632 children under five years of age who only make an average of 1,013 or 61 per cent. Deducting these figures the aver- age attendance for those children over five years of age would be 11,627-1,043=10,584; and 13,363-1,632= 11,731 on books, or a percentage of 00 for those over five years of age. This creates a record attendance for the borough, and places it as one of the highest for per- centage of attendance, instead of being one of the lowest in the County Boroughs, as it was a few years ago. I would also point out to your committee the fact that the number of children on the books of the various schools in the borough in proportion to the 'poPulatiou is 208, placing the County Borough of Warrington in the eighth place in the County Boroughs of this country. This is an important point in calculating the percentage of attendance There are 345 children residing in the borough who attend the undermentionedschools outside the borough boundary. There are also 420 children attending the Grammar• School, Blue Coat School, and ithe several private schools in till borough, making a total of .14,148. There are, however, 160 children attend- ing elementary and private schools in the borough Who reside outside, and this number must be deducted from the total, giving an attendance of children within the borough at 13,988.
LABOUR BUREAU FOR GIRLS AND BOYS.

This is the fourth year of the existence of the above, and it has been more successful than ever. I have been able to find some 250 boys and girls situations. It is the means of stopping to A great extent, illegal employ- ment. and employers will not engage a chilcr unless the certificate is countersiped by me." The Chief Inspector s report adds the Chairman is very satisfactory. Yet the average attendance might have been increased had there been sufficient accom- modation forschool-going children. PAST CHAIRMEN.

The Inspector also states :—Since the formation of the Committee four gentlemen have filled the chair, viz :-1877, to 10th April 1889, Mr. Alderman Webster, 1889, April to 13th August, 1889, Mr. Councillor Thomas Jolley, 1889, August to November, 1893, Mr. Councillor Fleming, 1893, November, to March,l9o3, Mr. Alderman Shaw Green. . Your committee will note that-in 1878 the School accommodation for the whole of the Borough was 8,258 and at the present time, March 1903, it is 13,596, an increase in 25 years of 5,328, whilst the average atten- dance for the same period has increased by 8,100. I have not the slightest hesitation in asserting that if more accommodation had been provided two years ago the total numbers on the booksand the average atten- dance would be considerably higheras there has been for a long time great difficulty in getting children of the poorer classes admitted in school. Your committee will be pleased to hear that the prosecutions during the past quarter create a record, it only being necessary to sommon 27 parents before the Magistrates against 51 for the same period of last year. The committee in relinquishing its duties, desires to thank the Council for the help and assistance which has always been readily given and assistance which has enabled the committee to carry out its somewhat diffi- cult and unpleasant duties in a manner in which the committee thinks has been efficient. The committee also desires to express its satisfaction at the way its officers have carried out their duties. THE CLIAIRMAN'S SERVICES.

At a meeting of the committee on March 19th, the above report was approved and ordered to be submitted to the Council. The CtiAIRMAS intimated that the Ist April next had been fixed as the date the Education Act, 1902, would come into operation and that the present occasion would be the last time the members would meet as a "School Attendance Committee," whereupon it was resolved that this committee desire to place on record an expression of their sincere appreciation of the valu- able serriees rendered to the town during the past 13 years by the Chairman (Mr. Alderman Shaw Green),who has always taken the warmest interest in the Educa- tional welfare of the Borough.

div.head: King Accepts a Warrington Present.
div.p: The King Accepts a Warrington Present.

ISome time ago, -Mr. Bancroft, of Warrington for- warded for the King's acceptance a walking stick made out of 10,923 used penny postage stamps, and he has since received a letter from Lord Knollys, His 3fajesty's private secretary, stating that "His Majesty has been most happy to accept the walking stick." It will be remembered that the stick was exhibited in the window of Mr. Alfred Taylor's boot shop in Horsemarket-street and it is a curiosity in its way. The stamps have been pressed on to a steel rod and the pressure applied has been so great as to make the stamps perfectly solid. The edges were afterwards neatly turned with a lathe and polished. A similar stick made out of halfpenny postage stamp, and another made out of match boxes are now on view in Mr. Taylor's window, together with the letter front the King's private secretary.
