div.head: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.
div.p: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.
Speech by Mr. C. E. Parker.
The Bethesda Strike.

A meeting of Liberals resident in Whitecross and St. Austin's Wards was held in the Workingmen's Mission !loom, Thewlis-street, on Monday evening. Prior to the transaction of the formal business,Mr.b. E. Parker, President of the Liberal Association, addressed the representatives of both wards, Councillor Tinnion presiding. Mr. PARKER expressed his pleasure that the Prime Minister had that day stated in answer to Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman that he would allow a day for the discussion of the dispute between Lord Penrhyn and his employees. He (the speaker) had no doubt that the defence of the Government would be that they had done all in their power to settle .that unfortunate dispute and he had no doubt that to some extent that defence would be a correct one. Over two years ago the Board of Trade entered into negotiations with Lord Penrhyn to see if it were possible to settle the difference with the men. Lord Penrhyn replied stating that to allow an outsider from the Board of Trade to be present in regard to negotia- tions with his own workmen would be to form a pre- cedent which he could not admit in anything which he looked upon as beiag altogether his private concern. He (the speaker) thought the question raised was how far in the case of a private individual owning a valuable part of the natural products of the country they could look upon the matter as altogether his private concern. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that men in the posi- tion of Lord Penrhyn ought tel recognize that in a sense they were trustees for the nation—(hear, hear) that they controlled that which was a national asset, and that the nation had a perfect right to in- terfere if the trust that was reposed in such men was in any way abused. He (Mr. Parker) was asked some time ago to take the chair at a Penrhyn choir concert. He did not consent to do so on the ground that he did not understand the ques- tion of the dispute and did not care to take either one side or the other. He asked if the person who re- quested him to take the chair could supply him with an unprejudiced account of the negotiations with Lord Penrhyn. The information was supplied and he read through it very carefully. The matter in a nutshell seemed to be that while Lord Penrhyn

professed to allow the right of combination to his work- men he denied that combination having any effective development or control. It was no use saying that they allowed combination if they denied the right of that combination to speak for those it represented in any ' negotiations. (Hear, hear). Since that time he had . been helping in a small way to minister to those who had been brought to such sore , needs . owing to that unfortunate strike. It was a national question and he had noticed that in conse- quence of the decreased production of slates at Bethesda lan opening had been made for slates from America. ; Looking at the matter from a national standpoint,apart •I from its being an industrial sore, he thought they would • come to the conclusion that where any master or land- owner abused the trust that he held for ' ! the nation that trust would have to be either restricted or altogether taken away. (Hear, hear). Mr. Parker then alluded to the education question and asked his hearers to realize that the children were the most valuable assets which the, nation 'possessed. They ; should ask themselves the question whether allowing so ' much of the control of the secular education of the d children to be in the hands of representatives of , sectarian interests did not very seriously jeopar- dise the efficiency of education. Allud- ing to the provision of the Act which allow-ed ' I four managers of each school to be repre- • sentatives of sectarian interests, Mr. Parker said ' his objection to this management by the churches was • that inasmuch as four managers were elected to repre- sent the churches the natural tendenoy was to make the interests of the churches and creeds the first considera- '' Von and to make the question of the efficiency of secular education a secondary consideration. That was a condition of things which was altogether objectionable and detrimental to the interests of education. I If the schools had been erected like Sunday schools to • , give this sectarian teaching, and the nation had ,not , ! taken the education of the children into its own hands, Ithe question would he altogether different. As this • was not the case he contended that it was distinctly to the disadvantage of education that so much control should be placed in the hands of representatives of sec- tarian interests. (Hear, hear). Speaking of the consti- tution of the Education Committee Mr. Parker pointed out that the members of the Town Council who had been elected on the authority were not originally ap- pointed on the Town Council to deallwith educational questions. Did they think that in the future the educa- tion of their children would form a very important part in the election of a candidate in the municipal elec- tions? The electors would not know whether theYwere voting fora man who would be placed on the Education Committee or not. He feared the question of education would have . very little effective influence in the elections. Lately the question at the ' elections had been whether a candidate was a trader or a non-trader and that question would probably be the ' burning question for some time to come. Education • would be altogether shunted to one side. In regard to I the co-opted members, they were selected very largely from the same sectarian interests as the boards of ' management they would have to look after. He con- tended thatthe other representation was entirely inade- quate. If the Chamber of Commerce had a representative ' why should not the shop-keeping interest, which was a much larger interest than the Chamber of Commerce, be represented? He did not object to the Chamber of Commerce having a member but on the same ground the shop-keeping interest ought to have one. Then again, why should not the iron workers Union have a member, and if the iron workers why not the tanners? If the tanners had a member why should not the publicans who had a large interest in the town and had children to be educated? To get a thoroughly good representa- tion of the whole of the inhabitants they would have to ' co-opt representatives of practically all interests which would be absurd. Would it not be a far better , plan if instead of having this authority which was so far out of touch with the electors, the parents and the ratepayers, they allowed each ratepayer to have a vote gin the constitution of the authority? The system introduced by the Aot was such a complicated, unfair, and unreasonable plan. Mr. Parker referred to the letter written by Mr. Perks, M.P., in regard to the Chertsey election and said he thought the position taken up by Mr. Perks was a most unfortunate one. It was one of those things which were rather apt to weaken the strength of the Liberal party. In regard to the Irish question, they , knew the Home Rule Bill introduced by the late Mr. Gladstone was it thing of the past and they might call it dead. He (Mr. Parker) and, he trusted, his hearers would ever be loyal to the great principle of sympathy with the Irish people which gav9 that Bill its birth. Although it might not be a particularly popular cry he did not think they as Liberals ought to be going about trying to get hold of popular cries. The Liberal creed ought to be deeper than that. They ought to have established convictions and be loyal to those convictions. He did not know in what form Irish: self government would come. It might possibly come from the other party. It would be rather disappointing to the Liberal party if after they had been working in that direction for so many years the fruit of their work should be plucked and eaten by the other party. The main thing, however, was that the Irish people should have their rights. They should put aside their feelings in the matter and if any government brought in a sensible measure of Irish self-government the measure ought to receive the approval of the Liberal party. Mr. Parker then alluded to the Sugar Convention and said that to his mind the arrangement arrived at, was the most insane arrangement that any Government could enter into. ,He explained the de- cision to abolish the bounties paid by foreign countries and said the effect would be to raise the price of sugar. He did not think the question had received the attention from the rank and file of the Liberal party that it deserved. The speaker briefly referred to the question of the taxation of land values and expressed his approval of Dr. Macnamara's pro- posal, which practically provided that a fraction of the inerease of the value of the land should go back to the people who produced that increase. Was it not an absurd thing that the people who increased the value of land should pav for the increase which they themselves had created'? In conclusion he asked his hearers to do their utmost for the advancement of the Liberal cause. Although their object was to return at Liberal candidate for Warrington, he would not have them think that that was the Alpha and the Omega of the preaching and prac- tising of Liberal principles. What they ought .to do was when they were convinced that a thing was right to spread the truth and the light amongst those by whom they were surrounded. .It was, however, a good thing to have a definite aim and purpose, and the aim they had in view was to return a Liberal candidate for War- rington. (Applause). A vote of thanks having been accorded to Mr. Parker the formal business was proceeded with. Councillor Tinnion was elected • chairman of St. Austin's Ward in place of Councillor William Roberts, who retired, and whose name was placed on the list of vice-chairmen. The secretary and committee were re-appointed. Coun- cillor James Evans was re-appointed chairman of White- •cross Ward.

The Liberal Ward me3tings for the Town Hall and Bewsey Wards were held in the Wycliffe schools on Monday- evening. Mr. O'Brien presidad over the former, and was re-elected chairmen for the year, the other officer being also re-elected. Mr. .T. Oxen was re- appointed chairman of the B3WA',Ay I‘,'lr 1. Mr. C. E. Parker delivered an address'.

A race of battleships took plane last week when the fleet was returning from Corfu, with the interesting result that 1-1.111.5. London proved to be the fastest battleship in the Mediterranean. While entertaining her friends at supper Mrs. Erdine Cretor. of Kokomo. Indiana, was killed by the explosion of a coffee-pot. The utensil, which was of granite iron, burst into many fragments, one of which struck her upon the temple and instantly killed her. All the guests were scalded and more or less hurt.

div.head: GRANARY OF THE EMPIRE.
div.p: THE GRANARY OF THE EMPIRE.
AMERICA'S INDUSTRIAL INVASION
OF CANADA.
[BY Mit. H. WIIITILIII.]

A series of letters written by Mr. Arnold White, for the "Daily Dispatch," and now published in book form, make very interesting reading for those who care t.) know what " efficiency " means. The following extract may be taken as the text to what I propose to extract from an American serial, "The World's Work" for the benefit of those who are on the look-out for opportunities of bettering their condition. Mr. White says :—" With such resources as those contained within the circuit of the British Empire, there is no reason why the destitute English should be exposed to the weather in the parks of the Metropolis or on the seats outside the Infirmary of Manchester."

Mr. Montgomery, the writer of the article in "The World's Work" referred to, says :--" The etory begins at the Atlantic threshold of Canada and pro- ceeds to the Pacific Ocean, with American achieve- ments all the way. And how did it begin? What, for example, called Mr. Whitney, of Boston, from his finished task of giving Boston a rapid transit system, to a black and obscure coal village in Nova Scotia, and how did he manage great steel plants there? He found the situation in Nova Scotia unique. In no other part of the civilized world is there a tide-water district where iron ore, limestone and coal are found so • cloSe together, so good and so easily obtained. Coal • could be mined and put on shipboard at less than 4s. a ton. Limestone and iron ore were handy and he set to work. - As mining lands in Canada are merely leased to operators who pay such high royalties that one-third of the Govern- ment revenue of Nova Scotia comes from the mines alone, it was necessary first to give strong guarantees to pay large royalties. He gave them. Next the vari- ous Sydney coal companies were consolidated into the Dominion Coal Company and affiliated with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Limestone quarries were secured, and at Great Belle rsland immense deposit's, yielding fifty-three per cent of iron were obtained, lying so close to the water's edge that the cakes of ore were shoveled directly into the holds of the ships. Cargoes of iron ore are delivered' at Sydney from the Wabana mines for less than ss. a ton. -Stephen Jeans, an English authority, computes the cost of manufacturing hematite iron at the great- est steel centres of the world as follows : West Cum- berland, England, £3 2s. 7d. a ton ; Westphalia, Germany, 14s. a ton ; Pittsburgh, America, £1 18s. 6d. a ton. At Sydney the cost is .tl. 10s. a ton without deducting the government bonus of us. on each ton of native ore and is. a ton for foreign iron manufactured in Canada which would lower the net cost to £1 2s. 7d. or 19s. a ton according to the source of the ore. This was Mr. Whitney's discovery in Canada. When the works at Sidney are completed, they will turn out half a million tons of steel a year,and al-ready plans are on foot to begin ship building there." Those who are interested in Empire building will do well to study these figures out and mark the con- trast.- Sydney is 1,200 miles nearer European ports than Baltimore, the port nearest Pittsburgh, 2,300 miles nearer Liverpool than Pensacola, the port nearest the Alabama iron district, and, through the fact, not usually borne in mind, that South America lies far to the east of the United States, 600 miles nearer to Rio:Janiero, than New Orleans and Mobile. It is also 900 miles nearer Cape Town than these Gulf ports are. In fact it is the nearest port to any- where. The Marconi wireless telegraph station is in this neighbourhood, and who shall say what this corner of the British Empire with its immense natural resources may become in its near future? And yet it might still be slumbering but for the American industrial pioneers. Quebec and Oatario have in their vast lakes and streams the largest reservoirs of hydraulic energy in the world, and American push is utilizing it all. The standing timber of Canada equals that of the whole of the European continent and is nearly double that of the Uaited States, and when we consider the immense business interests that are centered in such a timber region as this is we shall understand the reason why the attention of the peoples of the British Isles should .be kept steadily turas& tow-ssits • it. Of tlr,:so Isrest.s._ a large portion is spruce, white and black, the best material for wood-pulp, used for paper and 'other commodities ranging from ear-wheels and water buckets to buttons. Millions of American dollars are beinc, expended yearly on bilge pulp mills fitted up with the best American machinery, and large Owns are springing up around the once lonely cataracts,and it. is estimated that of the number who will enter Canada during the present fiscal year fully 25,000 will be, emigrants from the United States. I can find no reference to British capital migrating ,to Canada. The American investor is making his position in Canada that of sovereignty in the paper-using world. Twenty years ago wood-pulp went into the manufacture of but eight per cent, of ordinary paper. To-day it is more than eighty per cent. It is of great importanca to weigh well this fact as the supply of Europeon and American timber is fast diminishing and the world's supply depending more and more upon Canada. Or the Canadian; side of Lake Superior Mr. Francis Clergue of Maine has established a business that in its developments and economical features are Simply unique. Representing a Philadilphia Syndicate he has under his control water works, canals, pulp mills, chemical and mechanical works, railroads, telegraph and steam lines, iron mining, smelting and blooming, and electro-chemical works with all their subsidiary works. One of his lines going right into the North- land will open up a country equal in area to one-half the State of New York, and we must bear in mind that • Canada has in the whole of her vast territory' fewer inhabitants than the State of New York. The company of which Mr. Clergue is the active principal, is pledged to bring in,and provides farm homes for 1.000 settlers annually for five years ;this is in return for the Goverrim.ent grant of 6,400 acres of laud per mile of railroad. •

When we think of this, and then think of the state- ment made by Air. Arnold White touching the hom- less destitute of Manchester who have no home but the Infirmary flags, wescim but wonder at the lack of good honest statesmanship. Had Berlin but half the opportunities that Westminster has the Monroe Doctrine would be no obstacle to colony buildings. Canada has spent enormous sums of money in canal 'building, by which sea-going vessels may penetrate ahuost to the heart of the continent. This was suffi- cient for a time, but soon an agitation for railroad development begun, ;tad the Grand Trunk begun to spread itself. This in its turn was followed by • the Canadian Pacific. The last rail of the line was laid fifty-four months after the commencement of the road by .the company, and in less than one half the time required by its contract with the government. The Canadian Pacific stretches right across the vast plains and over the mountains connecting with the Pacific coast.

• The goldfields of western Ontario have just begun to produce gold, and the prospects are that in -the output these fields will rank with the Rand. and the great Comstock 10de... Americans have done almost all the work in the mines; and the capital has been drawn from the states. Many miles are already in operation, though it iS hardly ten years since the geld- bearing quartz veins were diecovered when the Canadian Pacific lines were cut through. Shafts have .been sunk in many places, chiefly by American com- pressed air drills bought by America capital and operated largely by American miners. Al! these opportunities are within the British Empire. There is still another and greater reason why the people of the British Isles should recognize in *Canada their most valuable jewel. England always lives from hand to mouth. Its fertile fields have been abandomed to huntsmen in red coats, and it now looks to the United States and to Canada for all its flesh food. Owing to goiernmental neglect of agri- culture especially of the dairy interests, England imports nearly all its butter and eggs and most of its fowls. Indeed the Kingdom lives practically of food brought from foreign countries. When, during the Coronation ceremony, the visitors t ) Lendon read the illuminated legend erected at Whitehall, "Ciumairr the Granary of the Empire," they , read of a development that was being effected not by English emigrants,or Canadian pioneers,but by farmers from the ITnited•States.lt is now conceded that the bulk of the wheat lands of North America lie on the Canadian si'l.! of the boundary line. The western ! who it belt of Canada is estimated to equal an area o: 400 mile.: from north to south, and 900 miles from east to west. This daes not inebt to the cultivable area of Manitoba and the North-West territories. A compara:ive example will best give the impressioa of the vastness of this deep-soiled river valley. Saskatchewan,one of the most fertile districts:in Western America, equals in extent the combined area of Maine ,

div.head: LOCAL RECHABITISM.
div.p: LOCAL RECHABITISM.
Annual Tea and Public Meeting at
Brick-street Mission. - SPEECHES BY THE REV. H. DUNNIGO AND THE HIGH DEPUTY RULER.

Success attended the annual tea party, concert, and public meeting in conmection with Charity Tent No. 11 of the Warrington District of the Independent Order of Rechabites which took place in Brick-street Mission Schools on S tturday evening. Judging from the large attendance at this function, the lodge Is at present in a flourishing condition. Abut 200 sat clown to an ex— cellent tea, an 1 the attearl Luce at th 3 after proceedings was very satisfactory. The meeting was presided over by the Rev. H. Ditnnico and the urincip it speaker was Brother Dane in Kirkwood, of Belfast, the High Deputy Ruler of the Order. Thera were also present on the platform—Brothers Baxendale(P.D.C.R.),WHigginson, D. Reid, and NV. Wright. After the singing of an ode and the offering of prayer, The CRAIRNIAN deliverei a speech. He said he was very pleased to be with them to show his sympathy with thorn in their work. He did not know very much about their particular order but he had entire sympathy with two of their avowed objects, namely, to preach the gospel of total abstinen3e and to teach men to be thrifty and provide for those emergencies which sooner or later came to them all. One branch of the work he was specially interested in, and that was the juvenile branoh. If they could only keep their boys and girls abstainers until they were sixteen and then traasfer them to their adult branch, they had gene a long way in helping to inik3 sober men and women. (Applause.) It seemed to hint that they were going to have a great struggle before long. The brewers and publicans were summoning tin their forces and were being patted on the back by the Prime Minister and assisted in their work by the King. It seemed to him that very soon the temperance forces would be tested to the utmost :indite hoped when that time came the Rechabites would not be found wanting. •He trusted that not only the , Rechabites but the Christian Churches would rally round the temperance banner, because he considered that the gospel of total abstinence was a very important part of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was very much afraid that the Christian Churches of Warrington were not so aggressive upon the temperance question as they might be. In some of their leading Nonconformist pulpits there was a strange silence upon the subject. He was afraid a real temperance sermon was never heard, at any rate they dare not venture to escestain the feel- ing of their congregation upon the subject. Some time ago the Free Church Council passed a resolution condemning the action of the magistrates in trans- ferring the Green Dragon licence to Lovely-lane in opposition to the wishes of the inhabitants with the request that each minister would ascertain the feeling of his congregation upon the subject. He was afraid it was only too true to say that not one of their leading Nonconformist Churches dare submit the resolution. They might have read it but they did not take the feeling of the congregation upon the question.He did so himself to a crowded congregation. He offended a few and they had not been since but their seats had never been vacant. As long as he remained in Warring- ton he was going to take his stand on the subject, even if it meant emptying his church. (Applause.) But it would not mean that. He believed that when a man stood up for righteousness, truth, soberness and purity his work was •bound to be successful. If they looked tip and down the country they would find that the men who had done the most good and beeu most successful in their different spheres were the men who had taken the stand he had indicated. He wished the Rechabites "God-speed "in their work and trusted that with their combined efforts they would be able to make "this drunken Warrington of ours " a little more sober and a little more like the kingdom of Heaven above. (Ap- plause.)

The concert was then proceeded with, the opening item being a pianoforte solo "The echo of Lucerne by Miss A. Hill. The recitation "The mother-in-law, of Moses" by Bro. G. Whitfield created considerable amusement. Mrs. Moores creditably sang "The gift of Life "and Mr. A. Spruce gave an effective interpre- tation of " They all love Jack." Miss C. Hastings I delighted the audience with her sweet rendering of "The Swallows " and was heartily encored. Mr. A. Bennett skilfully played a violin solo and was recalled. An address was then delivered by Bro. 1). KIRK WOOD who at the outset, spoke of the great pleasure it had given him since his appointment to the office of High Deputy Ruler to visit lodges in England and to see the earnest work of many of the brethren. He proceeded to speak of the origin of the Order, and pointed out that it was formed some 67 years ago, and he was pleased to learn that the Charity Tent was started just a year later than the Order itself. He had not been able to learn much concerning the founders of the Order, but probably they were workingmen. Allud- ing to the rule of the Order that no meetings should be held at public-houses, the speaker said he had found since he came to England that the custom of Friendly Society branches meeting at public-houses lingered here still. 'ln Belfast there were branches of all the large Friendly Societies at work, and they would not find a single branch meeting at a public-house. (Applause.) As far as he knew, there was not a trade union branch in Belfast which held its meetings at a public-house. Public-houses were not the places for workingmen to meet to save money in, and the founders of the Order of Rechabites wished to establish a society which should he separate and distinct from public-houses. Speaking of the progress of the Order, Bro Kirkwood said it had especially during the past fifteen years gone on with a mighty sweep. It had crossed the ocean and had struck its roots deep down iii our colonies. Almost wherevec Britishers had gone the Order had followed, and a member of the Order leaving this country for the colonies could carry with him a letter of introduction and by that means find friends amongst strangers. Alluding to the aims of the Order, the speaker said it was a working people's teetotal bene- fit society. It was intended for working people—those who were in receipt of weekly wages and to whom loss of time meant loss of money and sickness meant the curtailment of home comforts. The Order aimed at benefitting the working people firstly by the encourage- ment of thrift, and secondly by the promotion of the principles of total abstinence. Bro. Kirkwood showed that by paving a small sum each fortnight the members of the Order could when overtaken by sickness obtain free medical attendance and medicine and a weekly allowance that would be sufficient to keep thewolf from the door. In regard to the principles of total abstin- ence, the speaker quoted the statements of judges show- ing what a great amount of crime was caused by drink. Mr. Chamberlain had also said that drink was our na- tional disgrace, our national crime, and our national scandal, and unless the country throttled the drink curse, the drink curse would throttle the country. He claimed that the Order was a necessity to working people. We had many Friendly Societies at work and he had never in his life thrown a stone at one of them. He believed they were doing a good work, and tending to foster the spirit of independence among working classes. He believed they had helped in thousands of instances to keep the families of workingmen free from the taints of the Union and to prevent homes from being broken up. The speaker laid particular emphasis upon the total abstinence principles o aheOrder and said it had proved to b one of the best and most effective helpers of workingmen. (Applause). Bro, KIRK WOOD then presented a handsomely framed certificate of merit to Bro. G. Ryder in recognition of his excellent work in connection with the Tent. The concert was afterwards resumed, Miss A. Hill contributing a pianoforte solo and songs being rendered by Mrs. Moores, Mr. A. Spruce and Miss C. Hastings Bro. Whitfield again recitedand Mr. Bennett played a violin salo. The ditties of accompanist were discharged by. Miss A. Hill.
A heart.v vote of thanks was accorded t the Chair- man and sneakers on the proposition of Bro. W. Higgin- son, sec!)n4:l by Bro. J. Schofield.

Thr;,e men in a. motor car mounted the step of the capitol at Washington last week. At the sixteenth step the chain of the vehicle snapped and the car ran back- wards into the street. The riders were not hurt, but- the police arrested them. _ _

Mrs. Dudley Scott, youngest daughter of Sir Wool- laston and Lady Knocker, was married in London on Saturday last, to Captain R. F. Lush, West Yorkshire Iteginnt. It Ns-ill be remembered that Mrs. Scott's first husband met with a tragic death in the Cotswold Hills SeN,Il months ago, when Will ia at Wilkes Will his n,,igh'•our an-I gust, with winon he was cycling,. shot Mr. Scott deill and afterwards committed suicide

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a wall-attended meeting of this Society 00 Sunday afternoon. Mr. C. Eccles presided and sp?ke' upon the blessedness of a near fellowship with Christ, and the strength derived by close contact with Him- The Secretary announced the ahsence of Mr. William Silcock svho was engaged at the Bold-street Foreign Mission services, and stated that he (the secretary) would deliver the address. Mr. C. Furness very effec- tively recited "The Newboy's debt," and the hon. Secre- tary followed upon the theme of the recitation. He re- ferred to the good which was to be found in all persons g and said that down in the hearts of the most careless and the most depraved there was a good seed to be found which had possibilitiesof a growth to a grand and noble life. This was illustrated in the story of the newsboy .and the speaker proceeded to dilate on the blessedness of Sunday School work. Tn referring to Palm Sunday he said they celebrated that day the great hosannabs to His name. The spirit of Christianity, he hoped, would continue to grow until the whole earth was tilled with the life' the beauty and the goodness of His holy life. Master Pearce, 13 years of age, who has become known in Warrington as the boy organist, delighted the audience with his skilful playing on the organ,and manY stayed to hear him after the meeting. Two new mem-- bers joined nuking the Ot LI mcaibership 457.

A farm labourer at Rippolongen, Switzerland, dis- covered a human hand while digging in the fields. The police were informed, and on search being made the body of a young girl named Brenner was found cut up inkcv innumerable pieces and buried in different holes in the field.

Arthur Barron, a New York youth, devotes practic- ally the whole of his time to sleep. Because his mother endeavoured to arouse him' for a meal last week he knocked her down. When charged at the police court with the offence he yawned violently, and fell into a deep slumber in the dock. The list of Mr. Bryce's twenty " Studies in Contem- porary Biography " (issued by Macmillan) begins with Lord Beacons&ll and closes with Mr. Gladstone. The others include men so diverse as Dean Stanley and Anthony Trollope,Stafford Northcote(Lord Iddesleigh),• and Mr. Parnell, Archbishop Tait and Cardinal Manning, with other scholars, statesmen, and divines. The historians are fully represented by Freeman, Green,. Lord Ap,t,on ; the lawyers by Sir George Jessel and Lord. Cairns. In every case the sketch is only briefly bio- graphical,for purposes of exposition, the writer's °West is everywhere to present a personal ity,a character—some times. but rarely, a career. And constantly the form of the essay enables the writer to set down penetrating views on the professions represented; thus in addition to Mr. Bryce's own special fields of politics and his- torical study, we have many interesting observations, on the function of bishops in the English Church, many on the types of legal intelligence, while two essays— those on Mr. E. E. Bowen and E. L. Godkin—give occasion to remarks on the work of schoolmasters and of journalists. It is, in short a book full of graphic and genial impressions of a score of men notable in marl fields, and it is enriched with a host of valuable °biter dicta.

div.head: VITADATIO
div.p: VITADATIO
THE MIRACLE WORKER. ANOTHER CANCER CURE.

Neerim South, Gippsland, Victoria, August 21st, 1902. To Mr. S. A. PALMER, Dear Sir,—l feel it only right that I should send you my testimony as to the merit of VITADATIO. I had been a very great sufferer for years, having undergone several operations. After the last opera- tion I got very ill indeed.suffered intense pain,could nob sleep : in feat, got so ill my friends all thought I must die. I did not know thenlwhatiwas the matter with me. I was sent to the Melbourne Hospital; my husband thought I would have died before reaching there. After being ill in the Hospital for six weeks they informed roe that I had Cancer, and told my friends that I had only a short time to live—there was no hope of my getting better. I was then less than five stone in weight, and was taken from the Hospital to a friend's house in an ambulance, so ill that I could not move myself in bed without assistance. My friend (Mr. Newton) persuaded me to try VITADATIO, which I felt rather loth to do. However, in the end he prevailed, and I did try it, and thought it was going to kill me straight out, fur it seemed only to increase the pain ; but aftor taking It for about eight or nine weeks I began Is throw up • pieces of stuff resembling lights. I would retch for hour. at a tinso,and;the quantity of stuff that same up was just wonderful. I was taking VITADATIO for a long time ; I think I took in all between forty and fifty bottles. When I started taking VITA DATIO my friend said," If it cures you it will be as wonder- ful as the raising of Lazarus.' It is now twelve months since I took any. and I am doing all my own work (general household work). I think it is only right that I should tell what VITADATIO has done for me for the sake Af any who may be suffer- ing in the same way. You may make what use you like of this: There are a great number of my friends who can testify that every word here is true. I am a very different woman to what I was when I started taking VITADATIO. and I have taken no other medicine.—Yours slnserely, (Mrs) A. B. OLVER. Tyler street Preston. Vie, September 5, 1902. S A PALMER, Esq. Dear Sir,—l have much pleasure in certifying to the truth of Mrs 0 Olver's testimonial I have known the family for a nuesbor of years. Mrs Olver has been a great sufferer. She was brought to my house in an ambulance from the Women's Hospital in a hopeless condition. Her desire was to die and be free from torturing pain. She was too far gone • for any help from the medical or surgical profession; my wife and I persuaded her to try VITADATIO arguing that if It did no good it could do no harm. After taking VITADATIO for a week or two she- seemed to be worse, yet she continued until little by little her appetite came back, and after a terrine struggle with vomiting and pain, began to mend, and is now I believe thoroughly cured from cancer. Mrs Newton would gladly answer any correspond- ence relating to Mrs Olver's ease. We are satisfied VITADATIO cured Mrs Olver. Yours truly. (Councillor) JAS 0 NEWTON.

Presentation to the Misses Rimmer. The Misses Rimmer, whose impending retirement ' has already been announced in the " Examiner," will leave Warrington next week to take up their residence at 13irkdale, Southport. During the past few days they have been the recipients of tokens of esteem from the pupils at present under their instruction, the teachers, and old pupils. Last Friday evening they were presented by a deputation attending on behalf of the old pupils with a very handsome barometer and clock bearing the following inscription :--" Presented to the Misses Rimmer, from the old pupils, Warring- ton, 1903. Accompanying this gift was an album ' containing the names of the subscribers. On Monday the Misses Milliner received another present in the shape of a beautifully designed silver rose-bowl from the teachers and pupils. The inscription was as ' follows :--" Presented to the Misses Rimmer on the occasion of their leaving Warringten, as a slight token of esteem, by the teachers and pupils April, 1903." The barometer and rose bowl were supplied by Messrs Eustance and Co. COM:MARCIA-I. FAlLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette." the number of New Bankruptcy Proceedings in England and Wales gazetted during the week ending April 4th was 74. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 41, showing an increase of 33, being a net increase in 1903, to date, of 46.
